## Task 11 — MDX compiler off the app shell: root graph 1207.6 → 703.0 KB ✅ ### Cause `packages/react-router-chat/src/components/ChatMessageBody.tsx` statically imported `MarkdownRenderer`, which compiles MDX **synchronously during render** via `@mdx-js/mdx` — hence the two acorn copies. The chat surface mounts from `GlobalLayoutHeader` on every route, so that 505.6 KB was hoisted into the shell and paid on every navigation. (Note: `ChatMessageBody`'s doc comment claimed the renderer "shows the raw string as escaped preformatted text (NOT parsed Markdown)". That is stale — it genuinely compiles Markdown. Corrected in place.) ### Fix `React.lazy` at the chat-message boundary, with a fallback that renders the raw body as preformatted text so content is legible immediately and upgrades in place rather than flashing empty. Chat is the right boundary specifically because chat messages **arrive over the wire and are never in the server-rendered HTML** — so deferring the compiler costs nothing there. The docs/plans/notes/skills routes SSR their prose, so they keep the direct static import and are untouched. ### Measured (production build, `--skip-nx-cache`, static-import graph) | | Before | After | |---|---:|---:| | Root transitive static graph | 1207.6 KB / 381.4 gz | **703.0 KB / 237.7 gz** | | `MarkdownRenderer` in root's static graph | yes (505.6 KB) | **no** | Acceptance: no static path from `root-*.js` to the markdown chunk ✅; root static graph ≤ 750 KB → **703.0 KB** ✅ ### A test-quality problem this change created, and fixed Five chat tests broke, which is itself the proof the boundary really defers. Four just needed `findByTestId` instead of `getByTestId`. The fifth issue was more serious and **would not have failed**: the XSS regression tests assert the *absence* of `

Task 4 assessment (full detail added to NARRATION.md § "Hosted providers: cost, privacy, reproducibility").

COST — measured from the scripts, not estimated: the 24 Season-1 scripts total 11,277 spoken characters after lexicon substitution (avg ~470/short; longforms L1=1,494, L2=1,242; all ASCII so UTF-8 bytes ≈ chars).
• ElevenLabs (eleven_multilingual_v2 = 1 credit/char): Free 10k/mo < one season pass; Starter $6/mo (30k credits) covers a season + re-takes; Creator $22/mo (121k) ≈ 10 season passes. Effective ~$0.18/1k chars but the monthly tier minimum dominates. Full-season repin re-render ≈ 11.3k credits ≈ $2 marginal, $6–22 real (tier).
• Fish Audio: pay-as-you-go $15/M UTF-8 bytes on s1/s2-pro/s2.1-pro (no seat fee; s2.1-pro-free is $0). One season pass ≈ $0.17; a repin re-render of everything published < $1. ~10x cheaper than ElevenLabs for this workload; cost is a non-factor for both.

PRIVACY — both providers are off-box and narration text describes unreleased work. ElevenLabs: privacy policy reserves the right to train on personal data, account-level opt-out exists ("Data use" menu), zero-retention is enterprise-only. Fish Audio (Hanabi AI Inc., Delaware): retains content "as long as we need it", no documented training opt-out or zero-retention. Recommended gate, written into NARRATION.md: hosted backends may only render script text that ships VERBATIM in a published episode (that text becomes public at publish anyway), rehearsal/drafts stay on Piper or say — this keeps the "nothing leaves your box" product claim intact because the claim is about the product path, and the marketing exception is bounded to already-public text. sendsDataOffBox per take remains the audit trail.

REPRODUCIBILITY — Piper: local onnx, reproducible forever. ElevenLabs: no voice-pinning guarantee, closed weights, no escape hatch if Brian changes or is retired; model version (eleven_multilingual_v2) is now recorded per take in timings.json. Fish Audio: hosted reference voices are community uploads and can be delisted (real risk for the pinned 'Slax' voice), BUT OpenAudio S1 has open-weight releases (S1-mini) — a self-hosted escape hatch exists if we keep the reference audio locally. Net: if either provider gets a GO, Fish Audio has the strictly better long-term reproducibility story and ~10x lower cost; ElevenLabs must win the listening test decisively to justify its weaker pinning + higher floor.

## Task — Surface the non-success outcome in the run detail UI

### A pre-existing finding: no run status was visually distinct from any other

The task required a `no_op` run to be *distinguishable at a glance in the history list*. Reading the components, that requirement was not met for **any** status today:

- `Badge`'s `variant` classes in `packages/react-router-shadcn/src/components/badge.tsx` are all **empty strings** (`default: ``, destructive: ``, …` — the real styles sit commented out below them).
- No schedule component passes the `color` prop.

So `succeeded`, `failed`, `cancelled`, `running`, and `queued` all render **identically** in both the run-detail view and the history table. Adding `no_op` to `RUN_STATUS_VARIANT` alone would have satisfied the letter of the task while changing nothing on screen.

The fix uses `color`, which `Badge` documents as *"a deliberate, stable set of named hues for categorical/status tagging (e.g. labels, chips) … Treat this list as a public, versioned contract"* — precisely this use case. That means every run status becomes legible, not just the new one.

### Changes

**`data.run-status.ts`**
- `RUN_STATUS_VARIANT` += `no_op: 'secondary'`, with a note that variant currently renders nothing so the next reader is not misled.
- New `RUN_STATUS_COLOR`: `succeeded → green`, `no_op → amber`, `failed → red`, `cancelled/queued → slate`, `running → blue`.
- New `RUN_STATUS_LABEL`: `no_op → "no work done"`. Raw status is the fallback, so only values that are not already presentable need an entry.

**`no_op` is amber, not red — deliberately.** The run executed cleanly and nothing broke; the agent simply reported it did no work. Colouring it as an error would be as misleading as the green it used to get. Amber reads as "needs a look" without claiming a failure, matching the migration's rule that `no_op` is terminal and *not* an error.

**`RunDetail.tsx` and `ScheduleRunsTable.tsx`** — both now pass `color` and render `RUN_STATUS_LABEL[status] ?? status`. One shared data module drives both surfaces, so the detail page and the history list cannot drift.

**`data.run-detail.ts`** — `RUN_STATUS_TO_JOB_STATE` += `no_op: 'completed'`. Mapped to `completed`, not `failed`: the process finished cleanly, so the log console should stop tailing rather than present the run as an error. Whether work happened is the badge's job.

**No fragment change and no codegen was needed here** — `status` is already selected in both `ScheduledJobRunDetail` and `ScheduledJobRunRow`, and it is a `String`, not an enum. (`schema.gql` and `__generated__` were already regenerated in the previous task for the field-description change.)

### Tests

Two render-level tests, each asserting the *distinction* rather than just the presence of a label:

- `ScheduleRunsTable` — a `no_op` row beside a `succeeded` row: raw `no_op` is absent, `no work done` is amber, `succeeded` is green, and the `no_op` badge is **not** red.
- `RunDetail` — same assertions on the detail page.

## Task 2 shipped — commit `1f335c6f`

Files: `create-skill-file.server.ts`, `sync-skill-links.server.ts`, `config/skill-create.ts`, `utils/build-skill-scaffold.ts`, `SKILL_CREATE_COPY` in `data.copy.ts`, plus three test files. Gates green: lint (0 errors), typecheck, 3910 tests passing.

### Two findings the tests turned up, both worth keeping

**1. The realpath containment check was wrong on the happy path — caught by the tests, not by review.** `isPathInsideRoot(expectedRoot, absolutePath)` realpaths its candidate, and `SKILL.md` does not exist at the moment the check runs (only the directory does, from `mkdirSync`). Realpath failed ⇒ the guard answered "outside its root" ⇒ **every** valid create was refused *after* having created the directory. Now checks `skillDirectory`, which does exist by then.

**2. `.strict()` on `skillFrontmatterSchema` does not do what the plan assumed.** The plan says "an invented key makes the file unsavable". It does not. `parseSkillFrontmatterForValidation` builds its object from an explicit **whitelist** of `name` / `description` / `disable-model-invocation` / `tags`, so an unknown key never reaches the schema and `.strict()` cannot fire. The real behavior is quieter and arguably worse: **the key is silently dropped at ingest and the author is never told.**

This does not change what the scaffold must do — emit only legal keys — but it changes *why*, and it changes the test. The refusal test is now an acceptance test documenting the drop, and the rationale comments in `build-skill-scaffold.ts` say "dropped", not "rejected". This is pre-existing behavior shared with the edit path, not something this plan introduced.

### Guard-list deltas from the task-1 decision

- **Inside-repo personal root** resolves against the nearest **existing ancestor**. Plain realpath answers `false` for a root that does not exist yet — exactly the first-create case the guard is for. Also treats "personal root **is** the repo root" as inside, which `isPathInsideRoot` alone misses (it is strict-prefix).
- The refusal fires for **both** destinations, not just `personal`: a repo-destined create still runs a sync that would abort on sync's own version of the rule.
- **YAML emission is not naive.** Frontmatter is read by a real YAML 1.2 parser, so a description containing `: ` would become a nested mapping and a description of `true` would become a boolean the string schema rejects. `buildSkillScaffold` emits a double-quoted scalar whenever a plain one is ambiguous, via `JSON.stringify` (an exact encoder for double-quoted YAML, not an approximation). Covered by table-driven tests.
- Added a **fourth** collision beyond `personal.sh`'s three: a slug already discovered on disk, with its own message (`slugTakenError`). Catches a lockfile-installed real directory with no lockfile entry.

`config/skill-create.ts` carries `SKILL_CREATE_DESTINATIONS`, `isSkillCreateDestination`, `SKILL_CREATE_FIELDS` and `DEFAULT_SKILL_CREATE_DESTINATION` (`personal`). # Task 1 — Transport evaluation rubric + comparison harness

Each spike (A = HTTP service, B = docker exec stdio, C = host stdio baseline) is scored on the 8 criteria below. Scores: **PASS** / **PARTIAL** / **FAIL** (+ a one-line note). Weighted so the fully-Dockerized goal and the agent_conversation auth tension — the two things that actually decide this — dominate.

## Scoring criteria (weight)

| # | Criterion | Weight | PASS means | FAIL means |
|---|-----------|--------|------------|------------|
| 1 | No host-Node requirement (fully-Dockerized) | ★★★ | Works with Docker only — no host pnpm/Node/built `dist/` | Needs host Node or a built package |
| 2 | Hybrid (host Nx server + Docker infra) still works | ★★★ | MCP resolves the host `openthrottle-server:dev` with no extra steps | Breaks the current worktree-dev norm |
| 3 | Worktree isolation (right server instance per prefix/port) | ★★★ | Each worktree's MCP targets ITS stack (or the intended stable one) deterministically | Cross-talk / wrong server / manual per-worktree edits |
| 4 | `agent_conversation_*` human-JWT path works | ★★★ | Client can supply a human JWT per call; the 3 agent_conversation tools succeed AND `ot_sa_` machine tools succeed | Only one token identity works (SA XOR human) |
| 5 | Cold-start / per-call latency | ★★ | Tool calls feel instant (<~300ms overhead); no per-call container spin-up | Multi-second per-call or per-session startup tax |

## Task 8 — Checkout cost reduced across every job

Option 1 (`filter: blob:none`) chosen, as the task preferred. Crucially **`fetch-depth: 0` is retained** wherever history is needed — only *blobs* are dropped, never commits. That is what keeps `nx-set-shas` able to reach an arbitrarily old `main` SHA, which a bounded depth would have jeopardised.

### Every checkout in `.github/workflows`, with per-job justification

| Workflow / job | Setting | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `continuous-integration` · `changes` | `fetch-depth: 1` + 2-SHA fetch | task 4 — tree-to-tree diff only |
| `continuous-integration` · `build` | `0` + `blob:none` | `nx affected` / nx-set-shas walk history, never read old blobs |
| `continuous-integration` · `nx-dependency-graph` | `0` + `blob:none` | same |
| `vercel-deploy` · `compute-affected` | `0` + `blob:none` | same (converted though gated off) |
| `vercel-deploy` · `deploy` | `0` + `blob:none` | same |
| `openthrottle-docker` | `0` + `blob:none` | `nx affected` for docker apps |
| `dependency-graph-scheduled` | `0` + `blob:none` | needs commit graph to commit snapshots |
| `nx-release` | `0` + `blob:none` | versioning/changelog read commit metadata and tags, not blobs |
| `docs-watch` | **`fetch-depth: 2`** | runs one `git diff-tree` on `github.sha`; full history was never used |
| `secret-scan` | **`0`, NO filter** | ⚠️ see below |
| `terraform-validate` | default (1) | no history needed; already minimal |

### ⚠️ `secret-scan` deliberately left as a full clone

gitleaks scans historical file **contents** — blobs are the thing being searched. A blobless clone would either miss them or lazily re-fetch every blob in history one request at a time, which is *worse* than cloning up front. This is the one job that genuinely needs a full clone, and I added an explicit `DO NOT add filter: 'blob:none' here` comment so a future cost pass does not "optimize" it into a broken or slower state.

### Verification — measured, and the first attempt was wrong

My first test cloned via `file://` and git printed **`warning: filtering not recognized by server, ignoring`** — the local transport silently ignores partial-clone filters, so that clone was fully populated (60 MB) and proved nothing. Re-ran against GitHub, which does support filtering:

| | `.git` size |
| --- | --- |
| Full clone (`--no-checkout`) | **43 MB** |
| Blobless clone (`--no-checkout`) | **2.4 MB** — 94% smaller |
| Blobless **after checking out HEAD** (what CI actually does) | **10 MB** — 77% smaller |
| Blobs lazily fetched by the tree-only diff itself | **+56 KB** only |

**`nx affected` project set verified identical — the requirement most likely to hide a silent under-test.** Rather than trust reasoning, I established equivalence at both levels that `nx affected` depends on:

1. **Changed-file list** — `git diff --name-only BASE HEAD` in the blobless clone vs the full clone: **byte-identical, 150 files.**
2. **Working tree** — both clones checked out at the same commit:
   - tree hash: `84a3f656…` ≡ `84a3f656…`
   - hash of the entire index (`git ls-files -s`): `743cf974…` ≡ `743cf974…`
   - 6817 tracked files each, `git status --porcelain` empty in both

`nx affected` derives its project set from exactly those two things — the diff and the working-tree file hashes. Both are provably identical, so the affected set cannot differ. This closes the "silently-wrong affected set would under-test rather than fail loudly" risk the task flagged.

**`nx-set-shas` still resolves the last successful `main` run:** it queries the GitHub Actions API (hence `permissions: actions: read`) for the run, then needs that SHA present locally. `fetch-depth: 0` is unchanged, so **every commit is still present** — only blob payloads are deferred. This is precisely why I did not take option 2 (bounded depth), which the task also rated more fragile.

### Requirement partially met

**"Checkout step duration recorded before/after"** — step *duration* is only observable on CI, so the before/after timing comes from this PR's own run. What I could measure is the underlying driver, and did: **43 MB → 10 MB of git data per job (77% less), or 2.4 MB before checkout (94% less).** With `build`, `changes`, and `ci-success` per run, that is roughly 100 MB of transfer removed per CI run.

**Saving:** no dollar saving now that runners are free (task 2); this is wall-clock and bandwidth. It compounds with task 4's `changes`-job reduction (92 MB → 6.9 MB).

## `workspace-settings-action.ts` stays green — and that is the correct result

The task expected the form parser to fail too, since it is the file that silently passed before.
It does not fail, because after the migration **it no longer enumerates anything**: it calls
`WORKSPACE_EDITORS.is`, which accepts the new editor automatically. A file that derives needs no
edit; only files that *enumerate* need one.

The bug is still closed, and closed more tightly than a compile error there would have:

- Before, the parser held its own `new Set<string>([Cursor, Vscode])` — a second, divergent list.

## Task 1 — ROOT CAUSE (confirmed + reproduced on origin/main 24cede22)

**Active build target (inferred, not the disabled `__build`):** the `@nx/js/typescript` plugin infers an active `build` target for agentic-utils running `tsc --build tsconfig.lib.json` (executor nx:run-commands). Its Nx `outputs` include BOTH the dist emit (`dist/**/*.{js,d.ts,...}`) AND `dist/tsconfig.lib.tsbuildinfo`. So tsbuildinfo is cached together with dist.

**The `__generated__` mechanism does NOT apply here** — workflow.ts / foreign-workspace-context.ts have no codegen inputs. This is purely a stale-incremental / tsbuildinfo hazard, as the task note suspected.

**Reproduced poisoning (the smoking gun):**
1. `rm -rf dist && tsc --build tsconfig.lib.json` → complete dist (52 .js + 52 .d.ts, workflow.js present).
2. Delete `dist/src/utils/workflow.js` but KEEP `dist/tsconfig.lib.tsbuildinfo` (simulates a truncated dist — a partial GCS cache restore, interrupted write, or a previously-poisoned cache entry).
3. Re-run `tsc --build tsconfig.lib.json` → **NO-OP. workflow.js is NOT restored.** tsc trusts tsbuildinfo (says project up-to-date) and never checks that the on-disk .js outputs actually exist.
4. Only `tsc --build --force` restores it.

**Why this permanently poisons the GCS cache:** once any event leaves dist truncated while tsbuildinfo is intact, every subsequent `tsc --build` no-ops instead of re-emitting, and Nx re-caches the incomplete dist under a fresh hash. This exactly matches PR #254: cached dist had foreign-workspace-context.js (importing ./workflow.js) but was missing workflow.js.

**The bind (why the obvious fixes are wrong):**
- Excluding tsbuildinfo from the cache → reintroduces the stale-`.d.ts` bug fixed in PR #212 (see typecheck-buildinfo-not-cached-stale-dts). NOT an option.
- Converting agentic-utils to source-first (drop build) → NOT viable: it's consumed by openthrottle-server (Docker type-stripping needs top-level exports→dist), developer, node-client, drivers.

**Contributing factor:** the `build` and `typecheck` targets both drive `tsc --build` over tsconfig.lib.json and share the same `dist/tsconfig.lib.tsbuildinfo` (typecheck uses `--emitDeclarationOnly`), so their emit states can diverge — though the primary vector is the no-op-against-truncated-dist above.

**Chosen remediation (feeds tasks 2 + 3):** keep tsbuildinfo cached (no stale-.d.ts regression) but make the build self-verifying: after `tsc --build`, a completeness guard asserts every non-test source module has a corresponding dist `.js`. On failure it self-heals with a `--force` rebuild and re-checks; if still incomplete it exits non-zero so Nx never caches a partial dist. This closes the reproduced no-op case at build time.

IDEMPOTENCY took four separate fixes, each a real bug the checksum comparison surfaced (all 52 tables now byte-identical across a plain re-run):
1. Most tables carry a BEFORE UPDATE trigger stamping updated_at=now(). An unconditional upsert therefore rewrote the rebased timestamps on EVERY re-seed — 227 plans would read "updated just now" on camera and take 7 would disagree with take 1. Every upsert (loader + the five hero ones) is now guarded by IS DISTINCT FROM so an unchanged row is not written at all.
2. updated_at is excluded from that comparison because the trigger OWNS it: the stored value can never equal the snapshot value, so comparing it reports every row as changed forever on any table --reset does not truncate (users).
3. Hero plan_output_stream did DELETE+INSERT with id defaulting to gen_random_uuid() — fresh ids every run. Chunks now get deterministic d0d0d0d0- ids.
4. --reset truncate list is now derived from the snapshot's own _tables.json rather than hand-maintained, so a newly exported table cannot silently keep stale rows.

Imported rows arrive owned by imported users while the recording logs in as the demo user, and most workspace surfaces are user-scoped — so repositories, tag rules and all 125 conversations rendered EMPTY, exactly the empty-state problem this plan exists to kill. # Task 5 — Server correlation + aggregation verified (no migration)

Reviewed `recordSkillUsageOutcome` (resolver + service) and `listOutcomeStatsBySkill`
against the new automatic feed. **Confirmed correct as-is:**

- **Aggregation** (`listOutcomeStatsBySkill`, service.ts): `outcomeCount = COUNT(*)`,
  `successCount / abandonedCount / errorCount = COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE o.outcome = …)`,
  `avgDurationMs = AVG(o.duration_ms)`. SQL `AVG` natively ignores NULLs, so `abandoned`
  rows (which the automatic path writes with `duration_ms = null`) are **excluded from the
  average** — exactly the intended behavior. Grouped by `o.skill_name`.
- **Merge** (`listBySkill`): the outcome map is keyed by `skill_name` and merged onto the
  start-count leaderboard by `skill_name`, matching what the UI reads. `session_id` /
  `tool_use_id` are stored per-row for future 1:1 precision but are **not needed** for the
  leaderboard grouping.
- **Filters**: same date window (`occurred_at >= start AND < endExclusive`) plus optional
  `o.scope` / `o.git_branch` / `o.cwd` equality predicates. The automatic feed populates
  scope (`ours`), git_branch, cwd, and occurredAt (Stop time within the window), so all
  filters behave for the new rows.
- **Resolver validation** accepts our feed: outcome ∈ {success, abandoned, error};
  durationMs null or non-negative finite; scope defaults to `ours`; occurredAt validated.
  Manual opt-in `error` and automatic `success`/`abandoned` all pass the same path.

## Migration decision: NONE for v1
`session_id + skill_name (+ optional tool_use_id)` are already columns on `skill_usage_outcomes`
and `tool_use_id` is nullable; the leaderboard only groups by `skill_name`. No nullable
correlation column / start-reference FK is needed — adding one would buy precision the current
aggregation doesn't use. (Revisit only if a future per-invocation join is required.) Backfill
remains out of scope (historical starts have no completion signal).

## Task 1 — Baseline measurement (COMPLETE)

**Method.** No app code changed. Curled the always-running built server on `:6021` (`PROCESS_ROLE=api`, main checkout) directly, one GraphQL document per field group, fragments scoped per document. Auth: a real JWT for the seeded `developer-e1e878@atlasworks.example` (the `OPENTHROTTLE_MCP_AUTH_TOKEN` service account lacks `settings:read`, so `skillTagVocabulary` and `workspaceRepositories` 403 under it — a real user token is mandatory for this measurement).

Subject plan: `3fa7442e-b80d-4d64-a20f-5580fed58932` — 8 tasks, 31 output chunks, 24 plan runs. The `developer-e1e878@atlasworks.example` user owns **8 checkouts**.

### Warm numbers (medians, n=9–15)

| field group | median ms | bytes | share of warm total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `plan` + `tasksByPlanId` (**critical pair**) | 26.4 | 9,584 | — |
| `workspaceRepositories` (warm) | 9.8 | 3,819 | — |
| `planOutputStreamChunks` (no limit) | 14.1 | 12,994 | — |
| `planOutputStreamChunks(limit: 200)` | 25.0 | 12,994 | — |
| `planRunsByPlanId(10)` + `recentPlanRunsMetrics(25)` | 26.5 | 5,133 | — |
| `ruleApplications` + `workArtifactsByPlan` | 29.6 | 87 | — |
| `skillTagVocabulary` | 27.0 | 1,796 | — |
| **whole `PlanDetailIndexLoader` today** | **22.2** | 33,358 | 100% |

**Read this honestly: warm, there is no signal.** Every group — including the whole query — lands in the same 10–30 ms band, and per-request jitter (±40 ms) is larger than any difference between them. The full query is not the sum of its parts; it resolves them concurrently and costs the same as a single field. **Warm, this route has no latency problem at all**, and the plan's per-field cost ranking in the description does not survive measurement.

### Cold numbers — this is the entire story

`workspaceRepositories` → `workspace-folders.service.ts:777` loops the user's checkouts (`limit: 200`) and calls `resolveInspection` **sequentially with `await` in the loop** (there is even an `eslint-disable no-await-in-loop` on it, `:787-790`). Past `INSPECTION_TTL_MS = 15 * 60 * 1000` (`:66`) each iteration runs a full `scanAndPersist` disk/git scan.

Forced cold by nulling `scanned_at` for the user's checkouts before each run:

| scenario | run 1 | run 2 | run 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `workspaceRepositories` **cold** | 1563.1 ms | 1341.2 ms | 1271.4 ms |
| `workspaceRepositories` **warm** (immediately after) | 9.8 ms | | |
| whole `PlanDetailIndexLoader` **cold** | 1329.8 ms | 1283.6 ms | 1282.4 ms |

**Cold ≈ 1.3 s, warm ≈ 10 ms — a 130× swing, and cold-full ≈ cold-repos**, i.e. `workspaceRepositories` is ~100% of the cold cost and everything else is rounding error. That is with only **8** checkouts and a sequential loop, so cost scales linearly with checkout count: a 40-checkout user is looking at ~6 s.

The 15-minute TTL means this is **not** a rare cold-start — any user who opens a plan more than 15 minutes after their last workspace read pays the full 1.3 s, every time. That is the common case, not the tail.

### Gate decision for the rest of the plan

The task said to flag anything under 20 ms so later tasks can leave it in the critical query. Doing that:

- **`workspaceRepositories` — DEFER. This is the whole win.** Removing it from the awaited path takes worst-case time-to-first-paint from ~1.3 s to ~26 ms. Tasks 4/5/6 are fully justified.
- **`planOutputStreamChunks`, `planRunsByPlanId` + metrics, `ruleApplications` + `workArtifactsByPlan`, `skillTagVocabulary` — all in the 14–30 ms noise band. None of them is individually worth a boundary on latency grounds, and the plan description's cost ranking for them ("join-heavy", "metrics walks taskRunMetrics", "whole vocabulary") is not supported by the data.**

I am **not** narrowing the plan on that basis, because those boundaries still earn their place on the plan's stated secondary goal: today any one of those fields failing 500s the entire plan page, and per-region `errorElement`s fix that. But the honest framing for the PR is **fault isolation for four of them, latency for `workspaceRepositories` alone** — not "five slow fields". I will keep the deferral for all of them (uniform loader shape, no special-casing, and the ledger fields are dead weight regardless since `PlanTabOutput` has them commented out), and say so plainly.

One caveat recorded for task 9's before/after: since warm-vs-warm shows no difference, the after-measurement must be **cold**-vs-cold or it will show nothing.

Non-goal respected: no change to the inspection caching itself. The sequential `await`-in-loop in `workspace-folders.service.ts:787` is the actual root cause and a genuinely better fix (parallelise it, or make the scan background-refresh instead of refresh-on-view) — that belongs to `agentic-utils-cache-hardening`, and I will note it there rather than silently widening this plan.

## Task — `.mcp.json` config defects: 2 fixed, 1 dissolved (and an earlier finding CORRECTED)

### ⚠️ Correction: grok DOES read `.mcp.json` — my earlier audit was wrong

Investigating item 3 overturned the grok finding recorded earlier in this plan.

I had concluded "grok reads its own TOML, never `.mcp.json`" based on `grok mcp list` printing *"No MCP servers configured"*. **That command only lists servers in grok's own TOML config.** `grok mcp doctor` tells a different story — it enumerates `.mcp.json` as a first-class config source:

```
Config sources
  ~/.grok/config.toml         1 server
  ~/.claude.json              1 server
  .mcp.json                   5 servers
…
openthrottle-mcp (stdio: bash ./scripts/run-openthrottle-mcp.sh)
  ✓ handshake OK (protocol 2025-06-18)
  ✓ 62 tools discovered
```

Proof it is the **project** file and not some user-scope config — the same discipline I flagged for claude: `maestro` appears in **no** user-level config on this host (`~/.grok/config.toml` has no `[mcp_servers]` sections at all), yet grok handshakes it. So `.mcp.json` is genuinely the source.

**Corrected:** grok `attachesWorkspaceMcp: false → true`, in the driver, its JSDoc, the capability matrix test, the codex-grok capability assertion, the `ScheduleMcpWarning` fixture, and the advisory copy (grok now listed among the providers to pick for MCP-dependent work).

**Evidence grade, stated honestly:** `grok mcp doctor` is grok's own account of its MCP configuration, but the agent-runtime check — spawn the driver's command and ask the model which tools it holds, as was done for cursor, claude and opencode — was **blocked by grok's free-tier usage limit**. Recorded in the driver JSDoc as a gap to close when quota allows.

**Codex re-verified, and its `false` stands.** Given the grok lesson I re-checked codex with a second independent command: `codex doctor` reports `mcp  3 server (3 stdio) · 1 disabled` — the same three user-scope servers, with no `.mcp.json` among its sources. **Codex is now the only driver that cannot reach a workspace's MCP servers.**

The transferable lesson: `<cli> mcp list` answers "what is in my own config", not "what will I load". Use the CLI's **doctor** command, and always cross-check with a server that exists only in the project file.

## Task 1 — DECISION: option A with a B fallback (2026-08-28)

**Resolve the target dir, record and exclude the resolved repo-relative path. Refuse only when the resolved path escapes the repo.**

### Why A is viable at all — verified, not assumed

Option A only works if `.git/info/exclude` can hide an untracked entry that lives inside a **tracked** directory. That was the load-bearing unknown, so it was tested directly rather than reasoned about:

```
git init; mkdir skills; commit skills/real-skill.md   # skills/ is now TRACKED
ln -s ... skills/agents-ralph                          # simulate injection through the symlink
git status --porcelain   ->  ?? skills/agents-ralph
echo '/skills/agents-ralph' >> .git/info/exclude
git status --porcelain   ->  (empty)
```

Excluding the resolved path cleans it. A is viable; the guarantee is recoverable without giving up coverage.

### Answers to the three questions the task demanded

**1. Target dir resolves OUTSIDE the repo → refuse that dir, with a warning.**
`.git/info/exclude` patterns are worktree-relative; a path outside the worktree cannot be expressed, so injection there can never be made clean. This is the B fallback, and it is the only honest option. The warning must name the repo and the dir. Note this is not hypothetical-only: a `~/.claude/skills`-style symlink would hit it.

**2. Two target dirs resolving to the SAME real dir → inject once, ledger once (dedupe on the resolved path).**
Corrected during investigation: this does **not** crash today. `ensureMaterialized` has a defense-in-depth `existsSync(injectedAbs)` guard before injecting, so the second pass finds the path occupied and skips it with `"Skipping <path>: a non-OT entry already occupies this path"`. The bug is subtler than a crash — OT's own first-pass entry is misreported as a non-OT occupant. Deduping on the resolved path removes the false warning and the confusion.

**3. `scanTargetOwnedSkillNames` must build its keys from the RESOLVED dir — this is the trap.**
It currently `readdirSync`s the target dir (following the symlink, so it lists the real dir's contents) and excludes anything whose `${dir}/${name}` key is in `ledgeredRelPaths`. Today that happens to work *only because* the ledger also stores un-resolved keys — two bugs cancelling out.

The moment task 3 records resolved paths, the two sides disagree: the ledger holds `skills/<name>` while the scan builds `.claude/skills/<name>`. Our own injected entries stop matching, get classified as **target-owned**, and are then dropped from the manifest at resolve time — silently uninjecting the repo. Both sides must move together in the same change, or the fix is worse than the bug.

### Scope note

The repo's own skills are still protected: target-owned detection is what keeps them out of the manifest, and it keeps working as long as its keys are resolved alongside the ledger's.

## Task 4 — Sharded test invocation wired into continuous-integration.yml

### What the step now does

The single `selector="$(…)"` capture becomes a `key=value` parse of the partitioner's four outputs, then three guarded invocations:

```bash
[ -n "$selector" ]           → nx affected --exclude="*,$selector"     --target=lint,typecheck,bundle-hooks-check --parallel
[ -n "$testSelector" ]       → nx affected --exclude="*,$testSelector" --target=test
[ -n "$suiteShardProjects" ] → nx run-many --projects="$suiteShardProjects" --target=test --shard="$suiteShard"
```

The `lint,typecheck,bundle-hooks-check` line is unchanged apart from its `if` guard, and the general `test` line differs only in reading `testSelector` instead of `selector`.

### Drift between the Vitest shard and the project partition is now structurally impossible

`suiteShard` is **emitted by the partitioner**, derived from the very argv it partitions with — the workflow never rebuilds `i/n` from `matrix.jobIndex` / `env.jobCount` itself. There is no second place for the two to disagree, which is a stronger guarantee than the task asked for (it asked that they be derived from the same two values; this makes them the same *computation*). A comment at the parse site says so, so nobody "simplifies" it back into the YAML later.

### `--shard` is deliberately on its own invocation

Called out in a ⚠️ comment in the step: attaching `--shard` to the general `nx affected --target=test` line would shard **every other project's** suite too, running a third of each and reporting green. That is the same silent-pass disaster the whole step exists to prevent. Keeping it on a `run-many` scoped to `suiteShardProjects` is what confines the blast radius.

### The new third state is spoken out loud

There are now three, not two, and each prints its own line:

1. **no chunk, nothing sharded** → `🫙 Empty shard: … This is a no-op, NOT a skip`, exit 0 (unchanged).
2. **no chunk, but a shard to run** → `🫙 Box N drew no projects of its own. / NOT idle: it still runs Vitest --shard=…` — the new state, and the one most likely to be misread as an idle box.
3. **a chunk** → `🧠 shard i/n → $selector` (unchanged), plus `✂️ Vitest --shard=… of …` when this run also shards.

### Verified by dry-running the step's actual shell

The `run:` block was extracted from the YAML, `${{ … }}` stubbed, and the Nx commands replaced with `echo`, then exercised against five partitioner outputs:

| case | result |
| --- | --- |
| nothing at all | no-op message, exit 0, no Nx invoked |
| no chunk + shard 3/3 | "NOT idle" message, `run-many … --shard=3/3` only |
| chunk that drew the sharded app (box 2) | lint/typecheck with the app, `test` **without** it, `--shard=2/3` |
| chunk, sharded app on another box (box 1) | lint/typecheck + test on its own chunk, `--shard=1/3` |
| chunk, nothing sharded at all | exactly today's behaviour, no shard line |

- a failing Nx command **inside an `if` body** exits the step non-zero (only an `if` *condition* is exempt from `-e`, and none of the real commands is in one) → verified exit 1;

Live evidence (server at http://localhost:6021, read back via `plan(id){runConfigJson}`):

| # | How the plan was created | `workspace.repositoryId` | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| a9c5c0ee | MCP spawned by Claude Code with cwd = OT checkout | `08619f7c…` (OT monorepo) | ✅ correct |
| 88771d82 | explicit `workspacePath=/home/demo/Development/github/atlasworks/services/native-apps` | `fc184fa5…` (native-apps) | ✅ correct |
| 58c759f7 | launcher shim invoked **from** the native-apps cwd, no explicit path | `08619f7c…` (OT monorepo) | ❌ **wrong — the bug** |

### What the MCP actually sends

`packages/openthrottle-mcp/src/config/workspace-path.ts` already has the right contract:
`resolveStdioWorkspacePath()` = `OPENTHROTTLE_MCP_WORKSPACE_PATH` (trimmed) **else** `process.cwd()`.

`scripts/run-openthrottle-mcp.ts` destroys both inputs before the MCP process ever sees them:

- `process.chdir(root)` runs at the top of `main()`, before anything reads cwd;
- the server is spawned as `spawnSync('node', ['packages/openthrottle-mcp/dist/src/bin.js'], { cwd: root, env })` — cwd is pinned to the OT checkout again;
- nothing ever sets `OPENTHROTTLE_MCP_WORKSPACE_PATH`, so the override never fires.

Net: the child's `process.cwd()` is **always** the OT checkout, so every plan created through the global launcher is stamped with the OT monorepo regardless of where the author actually was. From inside OT that looks correct by coincidence, which is why the miss is silent.

### Server side is NOT the problem

`PlanCreationService.seedWorkspaceFromPath` handles the foreign case correctly today: SA → `resolveEffectiveUserId`, then `CheckoutPathResolutionService.resolveCheckoutForPath`, deepest registered checkout wins, explicit `runConfigJson` workspace wins over the hint, and every failure returns the run config unchanged (non-gating). Row 88771d82 proves it resolves foreign repos end to end.

### Client registration

`~/.cursor/mcp.json` (and the Claude block from `scripts/setup_mcp-instructions.ts`) register `bash <checkout>/scripts/run-openthrottle-mcp.sh` with an env block of 4 keys — no workspace key. Both clients do spawn the server with the open workspace as cwd (verified via `lsof -d cwd` on live MCP processes), so **capturing cwd before `chdir` is sufficient for the common case**; the env override remains the escape hatch for clients that launch from a fixed directory.

→ Fix belongs in the launcher (task 2), not the MCP config module and not the server.

All four tasks complete on branch `feat/scheduled-jobs-keyed-concurrency`.

**Design decision — advisory Redis lock, not BullMQ groups.** The plan asked to investigate BullMQ's grouping / rate-limit-by-key against the pinned version first. Both are **BullMQ Pro** features and this workspace pins OSS `bullmq@5.81.3`, so the plan's documented fallback is what shipped.

**Key shape.** Keyed on the run's resolved cwd (normalised), not `repository_checkout_id` — so a schedule targeting a checkout and one carrying a legacy free-text `cwd` that resolves to the same path collide instead of overlapping. That was the acceptance criterion an id-based key would have missed.

**Worktree question resolved** (the plan left it open): flag-only worktree requests bypass the lock entirely (the CLI picks a fresh directory per invocation, so no two runs can meet — without this the isolation the user asked for would buy them nothing). A *named* worktree is a directory two schedules can genuinely share, so its name is folded INTO the key rather than escaping it. A worktree request the driver cannot honor (codex/opencode expose no worktree flags and drop it) is ignored, because that run really does land in the cwd. The residual `git worktree add` against the parent repo is accepted unlocked — a sub-second metadata write to `.git/worktrees`, not the index.

**Crash safety.** TTL is 30s with a 10s heartbeat, deliberately far shorter than a run: the TTL is the only thing that frees a directory abandoned by a killed worker, so sizing it to cover a 15m run would block that directory for the same span. Release is a Lua compare-and-delete on a fencing token, so a lock that expired and was re-taken is never deleted out from under its new owner.

**Failure posture.** The lock is advisory — it defends against a git-index race, it does not enforce correctness. Redis unconfigured, Redis erroring, and (deliberately) nothing else resolve toward *running the job*. A deployment with `REDIS_HOST` unset has no lock at all, so the docs tell it to pin concurrency back to 1.

## Task — Chat and Ralph regression check: **both clean**

### 1. Chat — unaffected, and provably so

Chat cannot regress from this change because it never reaches the code that changed. Three independent confirmations:

- **Structural** — `grep` across every `conversation-backend/*/argv.ts` and backend module for `buildShellCommand` / `runDriver*` / `appendMcp*` imported from `@openthrottle/openthrottle-drivers` returns **zero hits**. Chat builds its own argv arrays and spawns without a shell.
- **Behavioral** — the full agentic-utils suite is green: **50 files, 541 tests**, including every backend's argv builder tests. No expectation moved.
- **By design** — the posture task established chat keeps its narrower, allowlist-based MCP posture (`--mcp-config` + `--strict-mcp-config` for claude, a scoped `mcp-config.ts` for opencode). That is intact and untouched.

No live chat session was needed to establish this; the change is provably out of chat's reach. Nothing regressed, and nothing silently gained access.

### 2. Ralph — verified live, on the real code path

Ralph's default backend is **`cursor`** (`DEFAULT_WORKFLOW_RUNNER` → `DEFAULT_DRIVER_ID = 'cursor'`), so Ralph is the largest beneficiary of the fix, not merely a bystander: every default Ralph iteration in a fresh worktree was previously running **without** OT MCP — while Ralph's loop is *defined* by `create_plan` / `update_task`.

Rather than retype a command, I drove Ralph's actual path — `runIterationAsync` → `toDriverConfig` → `runDriverAsync` → `cursorDriver.buildShellCommand` → spawn — after **deleting the worktree's cursor approval state** so it ran genuinely first-seen:

```
RALPH-BUILT COMMAND: cursor-agent --force -p "PROBE" --approve-mcps --trust

🤖 Running iteration 1
--- RALPH OUTPUT ---
Server health (GraphQL):
  api: ok
  database: ok
  redis: ok
  websocket: ok
```

Ralph attached `openthrottle-mcp` and completed a live tool call against the running server. `@tools/workflows` suite green: **43 files, 473 tests**.

No throwaway OT plan was created — a `health` call exercises the same MCP attachment path that `create_plan` would, without leaving data to clean up.

### 3. Capability-false drivers — no stray flags

claude, codex, grok, and opencode each have a regression test asserting their built command contains no `--approve-mcps` / `--mcp-config` / `--strict-mcp-config` / `mcp_servers`. The gate is `appendMcpShellFlags`, whose `false` branch is unit-tested directly (`utils/__tests__/mcp.test.ts`) since no driver exercises it end-to-end. **146 drivers tests green.**

### Decision owed — chat's cursor backend has the same pre-existing gap

Flagging rather than fixing, because fixing it is a call I should not make unilaterally.

`conversation-backend/cursor-agent/argv.ts:74` emits `--trust` but **not** `--approve-mcps`. Combined with task 1's finding that cursor approval is cached per workspace **path**, an interactive chat against the cursor backend **also has no MCP servers on any fresh checkout, new worktree, or container** — the same bug this plan fixes for scheduled jobs, in a file the driver tasks do not touch. It is pre-existing, not a regression introduced here.

I did not add the flag, because:

- `--approve-mcps` auto-approves **every** configured MCP server, and chat is an **interactive** surface where the user has not asked for that. The posture task deliberately preserved chat's narrow posture; silently widening it here would reverse that decision through the back door.
- Chat's other backends solve this with an explicit **allowlist** (`--mcp-config` + `--strict-mcp-config`). The consistent fix for cursor is an equivalent scoped mechanism, not a blanket approve — and cursor's CLI may not offer one, which makes it a design question rather than a one-line patch.

**Recommendation:** a separate plan for chat-surface MCP attachment, which can weigh blanket-approve against a scoped alternative and decide whether chat's cursor backend should reach MCP at all. Raising it here so it is not lost.

## Task 1 — Design gate: DECISION (owner confirmed)

**Source of truth:** Option 1 — `metadata.openthrottle-arguments`. A JSON string stored under the spec's free-form `metadata` map. 100% Agent-Skills-spec-compatible; non-OT tools ignore it gracefully.

**Per-argument schema (locked):** `{ name: string (kebab/identifier), type: 'text' | 'number' | 'boolean' | 'enum', required?: boolean, description?: string, default?: string | number | boolean, enum?: string[] (required when type='enum') }`. Arg-type union authored as an `as const` tuple, not an enum.

**Invocation encoding:** Option A — **named flags** `--<name> <value>`. Booleans render as a bare `--<name>` when true (omitted when false); values containing whitespace are double-quoted; empty optionals are skipped. Composed message: `/<slug> --arg1 value --flag2 ...`.

**Parser-path note (implementation constraint):** the existing `parseYamlFrontmatter` flattens frontmatter and collapses nested maps/sequences to an empty-string placeholder, so `metadata` is not reachable through the flattened `fields` accessor. The parser extension will parse the frontmatter YAML document directly (via `extractFrontmatterBody` + `yaml.parse`) to read `metadata.openthrottle-arguments`, then `JSON.parse` + defensively validate. Malformed/absent declaration → treated as no args (loader never throws).

Task 5 COMPLETED (d2b52e55).

The plan understated this task. `RepositoriesTable` used `getRowId={(o) => o.checkout.id}` and every cell reached through `row.checkout.*`, so "a discovered worktree that has no repository_checkouts row still appears as a row" is not additive — it breaks the row model's core assumption. I did NOT fabricate a synthetic checkout object to paper over it (that would have leaked a fake id into RepositoryRowActions, RepositoryInjectionCell and the drift lookup). Instead:

- `RepositoryCheckoutRow.checkout` is now `RepositoryCheckout | null`, and the row carries its own `id`, `displayName`, `path`, `updatedAt`, `activity`, `planId`, `planRunId`, `unregistered`. Row identity is `row.id` — the checkout id, or `worktree:<path>` when unregistered.
- `repositoryId` is nullable too, for a worktree whose owning repository is not registered. RepositoryNameCell renders plain text instead of a dead link; RepositoryInjectionCell renders nothing (no repository to flip the flag on); RepositoryRowActions returns null (every one of its actions needs a registered checkout).
- search/sorting moved off `row.checkout.*` onto `row.displayName` / `row.path` / `row.updatedAt`, so worktree directory name and branch are searchable.

Merge key is `checkoutId` from the discovery payload, NOT path-string comparison. The server already realpath-indexed the user's checkouts, so this is the authoritative pairing and a symlinked root cannot produce two rows for one worktree.

Deliberate: a row the scan did not observe gets `activity: null` and NO badge. Defaulting to IDLE would assert cleanliness we never checked.

Task 7 (ffmpeg assembly) — done, and the pipeline now runs end to end producing real files:

```
assemble: 03-first-plan — held 3.21s, 13 cues, portrait from a portrait capture
  03-first-plan-16x9.mp4  1920x1080, 25.05s, AAC stereo 48k, 1.14 MB
  03-first-plan-9x16.mp4  1080x1920, 24.99s, captions burned in, 1.29 MB
  03-first-plan.srt       13 cues
  metadata.json           title / description / tags from the script front matter
```

Everything the task specified is implemented and verified by extracting and looking at frames: narration aligned via the step manifest with the beat's **last frame held** when narration runs long (3.21s held here, never a speed-up); lower third burned in and the shared 2s outro appended; captions burned into 9:16 plus an `.srt` sidecar; per-beat region-of-interest reframing; optional ducked music bed; H.264 high/CRF 18/yuv420p/faststart/AAC 192k, now stereo.

**The biggest finding: reframing a 1920-wide capture into 9:16 is a losing game, and I could see it rather than guess.** Crop clipped the plans table at both edges; `fit` letterboxed it into unreadable 40%-scale text. So the runner gained a `--portrait` pass that records the same flow again at 1080x1920 and lets the app's own responsive layout reflow — stat cards stack, the toolbar wraps, every table row is legible. Assembly prefers that capture when it exists and records which source it used in `metadata.json`. Side by side it is not a marginal difference. Both reframe strategies are kept and documented, because each is right for some content.

**Three environment facts that shaped the design:**
1. **This ffmpeg has neither `subtitles` nor `drawtext`** — the Homebrew build lacks libass AND libfreetype, so `overlay` is the only text-capable filter. Captions and cards are typeset in the same headless Chromium that records the screencast and composited as PNG plates. Not a workaround to undo later: it means cards and captions share the footage's exact font stack.
2. **No SVG rasteriser installed** either — same answer, same reason (confirms the task-1 decision).
3. **No music bed is checked in.** `--music` works and the sidechain ducking chain is implemented, but shipping a licensed track is a licensing decision. A video with no bed is publishable; one with an unlicensed bed is not.

**Three bugs I introduced and caught by measuring the output, not by reading the code:**
1. **The frame-hold was malformed and silently stretched the video to 55.8s** (should be ~27s). A concat `duration` applies to the file line *before* it, so the held frame must be repeated first and given its duration second. Emitting the duration first produced two durations for one file.
2. **The concat list has to live beside `frames/`** — the demuxer resolves relative paths against the list's directory, not the cwd.
3. **The master was mono**, because `say` renders mono. Now `-ac 2`.

Also: the lower third overlapped the first caption at its spec'd position; raised it, with the reason recorded in the SVG so it does not drift back.

Refactored into `assemble/master.ts` so the landscape and portrait masters are one code path — they are different *sources* with different step timings, so the narration is re-laid out per capture rather than reused, and cue times stay honest.

### ⚠️ Found and fixed a silent-drop bug in the tag selector

Task 2 as written asked for the existing `!tag:name:<project>` shape. **That shape is broken**
and would have shipped a green-but-untested shard. Verified against the live graph:

```
$ nx show projects --affected --exclude="*,!tag:name:monorepo,!tag:name:openthrottle-email,!tag:name:@tools/workflows"
["@tools/workflows","openthrottle-email"]      ← monorepo silently gone
$ nx show projects --affected --exclude="*,!monorepo,!openthrottle-email,!@tools/workflows"
["monorepo","@tools/workflows","openthrottle-email"]   ← correct
```

Cause: a project's `name:` tag is derived from its package.json `name`, which is not always the
Nx project name. Graph audit over all 72 projects found exactly one mismatch — the root project
is `monorepo` but tagged `name:@openthrottle/monorepo`. `monorepo` **is in the affected set** and
owns `scripts/__tests__` (including these new tests), so under the tag form its
lint/typecheck/test would have run on no box at all while all three shards reported success.

Fix: name projects directly (`!openthrottle-server`). No tag indirection, no mismatch class.
A regression test asserts the selector never contains `tag:name:`.

### Added: shard-selector round-trip self-check

`verifyShardSelection()` asks Nx what the emitted selector actually resolves to and exits 1 on
any difference from the chunk it was built from — catching both silent drops and double-runs. One
extra graph computation per shard; the failure mode it guards is silent-passing CI, so it earns
the seconds. The comparison itself (`getShardSelectionErrors`) is pure and unit-tested in both
directions.

### CLI contract decisions (documented in the file)

- **Out-of-range `jobIndex` / `jobCount < 1` → exit 1, loudly.** That state means
  `matrix.jobIndex` and `env.jobCount` drifted apart, and the projects past the end would be

- **Empty chunk (fewer affected projects than shards) → no stdout, exit 0.** The workflow's
  `while read` loop then runs no Nx command, which is correct. Task 3 makes the workflow log
  "empty shard" so it can never be mistaken for a skip of real work.
- Diagnostics (the full 3-way partition, with this shard marked) go to **stderr** — stdout is the
  machine-read contract. This is the partition evidence task 6 needs in the CI log.
- Runner: `pnpm exec tsx`, matching `nx-circular-dependencies.ts`, replacing

# Task 1 — Design decisions (LOCKED)

## File name + location
- Root-level `.demo-workstation.local`.
- **Explicit `.gitignore` entry is MANDATORY** (not merely preferred): the existing `.env*` glob (`.gitignore:26`) matches only names starting with `.env`, and `.demo-workstation.local` does not — so it is NOT auto-ignored. Verified by inspection of `.gitignore`.
- Name deliberately avoids the `.env` prefix so nobody mistakes it for a real dotenv file that tooling would auto-load.

## File format
Annotated `KEY=VALUE` lines + `#` header comment block. Everything the helper persists is a plain key=value pair (greppable, no bespoke parser). Keys, alphabetized on write:
- `OPENTHROTTLE_ADMIN_URL`
- `OPENTHROTTLE_BOOTSTRAP_USER_EMAIL`
- `OPENTHROTTLE_BOOTSTRAP_USER_PASSWORD`
- `OPENTHROTTLE_DEVELOPER_URL`
- `OPENTHROTTLE_MCP_AUTH_TOKEN`
- `OPENTHROTTLE_WORKER_GRAPHQL_AUTH_TOKEN`

Header comment (regenerated on every write) states: git-ignored, local-only, values shown once at mint time (this file is the durable copy), and rotation steps (revoke via admin GraphQL → delete the line → re-run `pnpm database:bootstrap-service-accounts`). Never commit.

(Exact dev URLs/ports confirmed during task 4 implementation.)

## Write semantics + idempotency
Shared helper `upsertLocalSecrets(entries: Record<string, string>)`:
1. Resolve repo-root path defensively from `import.meta.url` (`scripts/` → `..`), NOT from cwd.
2. Read existing file if present; parse existing `KEY=VALUE` lines (ignore blanks/`#`).
3. Merge: preserved existing keys + incoming `entries` (incoming wins); union of keys.
4. Rewrite atomically: fixed header + alphabetized key=value lines.
5. `chmod 0o600` (writeFile `mode` only applies on create, so chmod explicitly).

Per-key upsert means the three required scenarios all hold:
- **(a) Fresh mint of both tokens:** credentials script calls helper once per minted account → both token keys written.
- **(b) Re-run mints nothing:** the mint branch is skipped, so the credentials script never passes token entries → existing token lines are preserved untouched (no clobber). (default-user still re-writes its own email/password/URL keys, which are non-secret constants/overrides — safe.)
- **(c) Partial (one minted, one skipped):** only the minted key is upserted; the skipped account's existing token line is preserved.

Because the helper reads-merges-rewrites, the two scripts running in sequence within one `setup.sh` do not stomp each other's keys.

## Permissions
File written mode `0600` (owner read/write only).

## Task 5 — BLOCKED: the ≤100 KB target is not reachable, and the premise is wrong

### The `rrule` premise is false
The audit attributed the chunk to "`rrule` + `Temporal` from `@openthrottle/react-router-scheduling`". **The `rrule` library is not installed anywhere in the workspace** (`find node_modules/.pnpm -maxdepth 1 -name 'rrule@*'` → empty). The 43 lowercase `rrule` hits are the `rrule` *property name* on schedule-x event objects.

`packages/react-router-scheduling/src/utils/recurrence.ts` says so in its own header — `buildRRule` is hand-rolled specifically to avoid the dependency:
> "The supported subset is hand-rolled rather than pulling the full `rrule` library … the extra dependency (and its bundle cost in a source-first package) is not warranted."

So there is no recurrence library to code-split out.

### What the 310.1 KB actually is (measured by ablation)
Stubbed `import 'temporal-polyfill/global'` in both `temporal-bootstrap.ts` and `datetime.ts`, rebuilt:

| Component | KB |
|---|---:|
| Temporal polyfill | **55.7** (Vite resolves `global.min.js`, 55.4 KB — exact match) |
| schedule-x engine + preact + calendar UI | **254.4** |
| **Total** | **310.1** |

**Even deleting Temporal outright leaves 254.4 KB**, so ≤100 KB is unreachable. The remainder is the calendar engine itself: `@schedule-x/{calendar,calendar-controls,current-time,drag-and-drop,event-modal,event-recurrence,events-service,resize,react}` plus preact. ### Gap 1: no retry on mint — FIXED

`mintCursorSessionWithRetry()` wraps the mint at the `runStream` call site:

- `CURSOR_MINT_MAX_ATTEMPTS = 2`, `CURSOR_MINT_RETRY_DELAY_MS = 500`
- retries **only** retryable failures, and never once the run's signal has aborted
- logs `attempt=N/2` and `kind=` on every attempt, so the server log now shows whether a turn was retried and why not

The classifier the task allowed for landed here rather than in task 7, since task 6 is what needs it — `cursor-agent/errors.ts`, exported from the backend barrel:

- `CURSOR_FAILURE_KINDS` = `authRequired` | `notInstalled` | `timeout` | `unknown`
- `classifyCursorFailure(message)` — patterns taken from output captured off the real binary in task 1, not invented. Ordering is deliberate: `notInstalled` first (an ENOENT message can also mention a path), then `authRequired` before `timeout` (an auth failure that also timed out is still the user's to fix).
- `isRetryableCursorFailure(kind)` — `timeout` and `unknown` yes; `authRequired` and `notInstalled` never.

`unknown` is retryable **on purpose**: the cold-start failures this plan chased match no pattern, and one extra spawn is cheap next to a dead turn. Auth and missing-binary are not, because retrying them only doubles the wait before the user sees the message they need to act on.

Task 7 now consumes this same classifier for composer copy, so retry policy and user-facing copy can never disagree about what a failure is.

### Gap 2: re-mint a poisoned session id — NO TRIGGER EXISTS

The task specifies: *"Detect a resume failure in `streamCursorAgent()`: when cursor exits non-zero with a 'chat not found' / 'invalid chat id' style stderr…"*

## Task 6 — Shared (Redis) discovery cache: NO-GO (deferred) ✅

Decision: **do not** back the discovery caches with Redis now. Keep the in-memory L1 (SWR + coalescing from tasks 2–3). Recorded here per the task's "if NO-GO, record + close" path.

### Why NO-GO

**1. Correctness — discovery is host-local, so a shared snapshot can be wrong.** Both scans measure the machine the server process runs on: `discoverAgentClis` spawns `<cli> --version` child processes (which CLIs are installed on *this* host/container), and `discoverModels` probes `localhost` / `host.docker.internal` ports (which model servers are reachable from *this* pod). In a multi-instance deployment a Redis-shared result from instance A would advertise CLIs/endpoints that may not exist on instance B. Even a homogeneous container image (identical baked-in CLIs) still has *per-pod* local model endpoints — an ollama on one pod's localhost isn't on another's. A correct shared cache would need host-scoped keys (`discovery:<host-fingerprint>:…`), which collapses back to ~one instance per key and erases the fleet-sharing benefit. This is the decisive reason: sharing trades a latency win for a correctness risk.

**2. The cost SWR + coalescing was meant to solve is already gone.** After tasks 2–3, only the *first-ever* request per process blocks; every later request serves the last-good snapshot instantly and refreshes out of band. So the "every ~60s someone pays the cold scan" problem that motivated a shared cache no longer exists per instance. Redis would only shave the single first-request-per-process cold scan — a once-per-deploy/restart cost, not a repeat-load cost.

**3. Added complexity vs benefit.** A Redis L2 adds: serialization/versioning of the snapshot, an invalidation story (currently `invalidate()` is a local no-network call), a config flag + wiring to `@openthrottle/nestjs-redis`, failure-mode handling (Redis down → fall back to L1), and tests — all to save one cold scan per process lifetime, against the correctness caveat above. Payload size is small (a handful of endpoints/agents), so payload isn't the blocker; the blocker is that the benefit is marginal and the semantics are wrong for a heterogeneous fleet.

**4. SETTINGS_READ scoping is not a factor either way.** The guard is authorization, not personalization — the snapshot is identical for every authorized user on a given host — so a shared cache wouldn't leak per-user data. But that only means Redis is *safe*, not *worth it*.

### If it's ever revisited (revive criteria)

Reopen only if we run a genuinely multi-instance/serverless server AND establish that instances are host-homogeneous for discovery purposes (identical CLIs *and* identical local endpoints, or discovery moves off-host). Then implement as **L1 (in-memory) in front of L2 (Redis)** behind a config flag, with **host-scoped keys** and the existing SWR semantics layered on the L2 read (serve stale from Redis, refresh one instance). Until then, longer TTL + SWR (shipped) is the right trade.

## Task 2 — failing regression landed (a90f17fc)

Two tests against `WorkspaceEditorConfigService` in a real temp git repo. One fails on this commit, which is the bug; the other passes and pins the distinction the fix must preserve.

### Correction to this task's stated requirement

The task asked for a test asserting **`git status --porcelain` stays EMPTY**. Writing it surfaced that this is the wrong goal, and asserting it would have been actively harmful.

Applying editor config also writes `.cursor/mcp.json`, which is a **new untracked file in the user's repo** — and that is correct. They asked for it. The first draft failed with:

```
expected '?? .cursor/\n?? .openthrottle/' to be ''
```

Only the second entry is residue. The first is the deliverable.

Had the requirement been implemented literally, the obvious way to make it pass would have been to exclude everything the apply writes — hiding the user's own MCP config from them, which is a worse bug than the one being fixed, and it would have looked green.

So the invariant is narrower and truer: **OT's own bookkeeping never appears in the user's `git status`; anything the user asked for stays visible.** The tests assert exactly that, via `git check-ignore` per path rather than a whole-status equality:

- `.openthrottle/workspace-editors.json` → ignored, and absent from `git status` **(fails today)**
- `.cursor/mcp.json` → **not** ignored, and present in `git status` **(passes today)**

This also matches the original report: `ssm-data-pipeline` showed only `?? .openthrottle/`, because its MCP config was already settled.

### Baseline

The fixture builds and commits the whole layout — including `scripts/run-openthrottle-mcp.sh`, without which the service warns and skips MCP config entirely — **before** applying, and asserts `porcelain() === ''` first. Same gotcha as OT b409da6e: a layout created after the initial commit makes the baseline dirty and the result meaningless.

## 1. Config surface — DECIDED

**Put `merge_queue` on ruleset `main` (id 14604876). Do not enable the classic-protection "Require merge queue" toggle.**

Why:
- Ruleset is already the richer, API-manageable surface (`required_linear_history`, `non_fast_forward`, `deletion`, `pull_request`).
- Classic branch protection currently owns the only required check (`ci-success`); leave it there for this flip so a stall has one candidate cause.
- Follow-up (separate change, not this plan's enable task): migrate `required_status_checks: [ci-success]` onto the ruleset so there is a single place to read. Explicitly **out of scope for the enable flip**.

## 2. Queue merge method — RECOMMENDED SQUASH (HUMAN GATE)

**Recommendation: `SQUASH`.** Awaiting explicit human confirmation before any later task applies it.

Ruled out: `MERGE` — incompatible with ruleset `required_linear_history`.

### SQUASH (recommended)

- Commit shape on `main`: one rewritten commit per PR.
- Title comes from repo setting `squash_merge_commit_title: PR_TITLE` (must stay conventional-commit).
- Body comes from `squash_merge_commit_message: COMMIT_MESSAGES` — preserves per-task messages including `Plan-Id:` / `Task-Id:` footers.
- Matches OT work-ledger language everywhere ("record the landed squash commit" / `workflow-link-merge`).
- Matches agentic multi-commit PRs: N task commits → one landed SHA for ledger recording.

### REBASE (alternative)

- Every individual PR commit lands on `main` (rewritten SHAs).
- Each commit must already be conventional; footers survive per-commit.
- Aligns with today's ruleset `pull_request.allowed_merge_methods: ["rebase"]` without touching that rule.
- Conflicts with documented "one squash SHA on main" ledger model — agents would need to pick the tip of the rebased series, not a squash SHA.

### Queue method vs ruleset `allowed_merge_methods`

They are configured independently, but leaving them disagreed is a footgun.

- Today: ruleset allows **rebase only**; repo also has squash enabled at the repo-settings layer.
- If queue = **SQUASH**: task 4 must also expand ruleset `pull_request.allowed_merge_methods` to include `squash` (prefer `["squash"]` to match the queue, or `["squash","rebase"]` if a non-queue escape hatch is wanted). That is a companion edit to the merge_queue rule, not a status-check migration.
- If queue = **REBASE**: leave `allowed_merge_methods: ["rebase"]`; methods agree; ledger/docs wording becomes the follow-up debt.

**Human: reply SQUASH or REBASE to unlock task 4.**

## 3. Tuning knobs — DECIDED (pending only merge_method)

| Knob | Value | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `merge_method` | **SQUASH** (pending confirm) | See §2 |
| `max_entries_to_build` | **5** | GitHub default; free public runners; enough speculative parallelism without a stampede on a still-small queue |
| `min_entries_to_merge` | **1** | Do not delay single PRs to batch; agents/humans want land latency; batching widens the semantic-conflict window |
| `max_entries_to_merge` | **5** | Default upper bound if the queue is busy; harmless with min=1 |
| `min_entries_to_merge_wait_minutes` | **0** | With min=1 we never wait for a cohort; make that explicit rather than inheriting the 5-minute default |
| `check_response_timeout_minutes` | **60** | Build shard ceiling is `timeout-minutes: 30`; projected 3-way shard ~10.6m; pre-shard fat-main worst case 28m24s. The required context is `ci-success`, which waits for all shards. Timeout must exceed the job ceiling with headroom or healthy entries dequeue. 60 = GitHub default and clears 30m + setup/aggregation slack |
| `grouping_strategy` | **ALLGREEN** | Same diagnosability ethos as `fail-fast: false` on shards: know which entry broke. HEADGREEN saves CI but obscures blame |

**When to roll back:** queue entries timing out / dequeueing without a clear CI failure; `main` unable to merge; merge_group runs never reporting `ci-success`; footers or conventional titles destroyed on land.

# Spike A (HTTP-service transport) — findings so far

## Feasibility: CONFIRMED (from @rekog/mcp-nest 1.9.9 source + a live boot attempt)
- The lib auto-registers a **STREAMABLE_HTTP** controller at `POST /mcp`, defaulting to **stateless JSON mode** (`statelessMode:true, enableJsonResponse:true`) — a plain JSON POST works; no SSE session required.
- The Nest module here (`NestjsMcpDeveloperModule.forRoot`) already accepts `transport`; only the runner hardcodes STDIO. Wrote a throwaway HTTP runner (`run-server-http.spike.ts`) using `NestFactory.create` + `transport: STREAMABLE_HTTP` + `listen(6022)`.

## Auth model for criterion 4: RESOLVED (design confirmed)
- `getAuthToken()` reads a **per-request** token from an AsyncLocalStorage store (`requestAuthTokenStorage`, via `withMcpDeveloperAuthTokenAsync`) and falls back to env `OPENTHROTTLE_MCP_AUTH_TOKEN`. So an HTTP **guard** reading `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and wrapping the handler in that store gives exactly the needed behavior: client sends a **human JWT → agent_conversation_* works**; sends `ot_sa_` / nothing → env-fallback machine tools work.
- Crucial differentiator: @rekog/mcp-nest **guards are HTTP/SSE only** — the lib explicitly warns `@ToolGuards()` are unsupported on STDIO ("Consider using HTTP transport"). So clean per-request identity (the criterion-4 win) is achievable ONLY on HTTP, not stdio. Strong point for A.

## Live-boot gotchas discovered (feed Phase 3 / the Docker image task)
1. **Nest HTTP path needs built workspace deps.** The module imports `@openthrottle/nestjs-modules` (LoggerModule), whose package.json points at `dist/` — not built in a fresh worktree → `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. The stdio `runServerLocal` avoids this by using a raw `McpServer` (no Nest). Implication: the `mcp` Docker image must build these deps, OR the HTTP runner should be built on the raw MCP-SDK `StreamableHTTPServerTransport` (mirroring runServerLocal) to stay dependency-light. Worth deciding in task 6.
2. **Needs `@nestjs/platform-express`** (added to the MCP package for this spike) — the package never needed an HTTP adapter before (only headless `createApplicationContext`).
3. Server URL resolution: the spike must point at a LIVE server; `${OPENTHROTTLE_SERVER_APP_URL}` in a worktree .env is that worktree's own (often dead) port — the same live-resolution the stdio launcher already solves via /health probing.

### 1. Plugin hooks fire under `-p` — ✅ VERIFIED
### 2. `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` resolves to the absolute plugin path outside cwd — ✅ VERIFIED
Every probe line reported `pluginRoot=<abs plugin dir>` while `cwd` stayed the target repo.

### 3. No-clobber — ✅ VERIFIED, not merely asserted
On every shared event **both** the target's hook and the plugin's hook ran, target first:
`target-SessionStart` → `plugin-SessionStart`, `target-PreToolUse-Skill` → `plugin-PreToolUse-Skill`,
`target-Stop` → `plugin-Stop`. Additive merge confirmed empirically.

### 4. Event survival under `-p` — ALL FIVE SURVIVE, but two runs were needed

| event | fires headless | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SessionStart` | ✅ | both runs |
| `PreToolUse` (matcher `Skill`) | ✅ | run 1 — model invoked the skill **as a tool** |
| `PostToolUse` | ✅ | run 1 |
| `UserPromptExpansion` | ✅ | run 2 **only** |
| `Stop` | ✅ | both runs |
| `SessionEnd` | ✅ | both runs (plugin only — target had no handler) |

**The one non-obvious result:** `UserPromptExpansion` did **not** fire in run 1 (prompt
`"Use the probe-skill skill now."`) and **did** fire in run 2 (prompt `"/probe-skill"`). It is gated on
the prompt actually *needing* expansion, not on headless vs interactive. Symmetrically, run 2 raised no

Consequence for the payload: `PreToolUse(Skill)` and `UserPromptExpansion` are **complementary capture
paths, not redundant ones** — a session hits one or the other depending on how the skill was reached.
Both must ship. This matches how this repo's own `.claude/settings.json` already wires them.

## Task 3 — 3-box project-shard matrix wired

`env.jobCount: 3`, `matrix.jobIndex: [1, 2, 3]`, `strategy.fail-fast: false`, single
`target: ['lint,typecheck,test']` (no target × jobIndex cross product). The single-box
`NX affected` step was **replaced**, not stacked — the full affected lint/typecheck/test no
longer runs on any box. The dead commented shard loop at the bottom of the job is deleted.

### Superseded task 2's `target` argv — reason

Preserving the parallelism split (`lint,typecheck,bundle-hooks-check --parallel` vs `test` at
Nx's default) requires the workflow to issue **two** differently-parameterized Nx commands. A
partitioner that emits `"<selector> <target>"` lines can only carry one parallelism per line, so
either the split dies or the target names get hardcoded in the script. Instead the partitioner
now answers only "which projects are mine?" — argv is `<jobIndex> <jobCount>`, stdout is one
selector line (empty for an empty shard). Which targets run, and how, stays in the workflow where
that reasoning already lives. This *removes* the quoting hazard task 2's requirement was guarding
against rather than mitigating it: no argv slot can contain a space any more. Tests updated
(`getShardLines` → `getShardSelector`); root `monorepo:test` still 210 passing.

### Once-per-run gates → `if: matrix.jobIndex == 1`

circular deps · GraphQL codegen drift guard · agent-asset SSOT · frontmatter validation ·
dependency-license gate · THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES freshness · prettier format-check ·
`audit:strict`. All read the whole tree or the whole installed graph, so their result is
identical per box.

Chose shard 1 over a sibling `gates` job: measured, these total **~20s**, while a separate runner
would pay ~1.6 min of checkout+install to reclaim them — plus a `needs` edge to keep correct. A
banner comment above the block tells the next editor which side a new step belongs on.

**Deliberate deviation from the requirement list:** `🧩 Codegen Tasks` stays on **every** box,
over the full affected set. It is a prerequisite for typecheck (a shard cannot know which of a
sibling's generated files its own projects import), not extra gate work, so it is not a cost that
sharding multiplies. Its `git diff --exit-code` drift assertion is then free, and running it on
all three boxes is strictly more coverage than gating it. Documented inline.

### Preserved deliberately

- `test` is **not** flipped to `--parallel`. Spreading projects across boxes says nothing about
  co-running two heavy jsdom suites on one of them; that stays evidence-gated (task 6 / plan
  e448a51d).
- `ci-success` unchanged — `needs.build.result` already aggregates the matrix ('success' only if
  every shard succeeded). Comment now spells that out and warns that the three matrix-suffixed leg

# Spike B — docker-exec / run stdio (lighter eval)

Approach: keep stdio, but run the MCP inside a container — `.mcp.json` launches `docker compose exec -T mcp node dist/src/bin.js` (or `run --rm -T`). No live mcp container exists yet (that's task 6), so this is evaluated from the known stdio behavior (proven earlier this session via the stdio-fallback driver) + a measured docker-exec cost.

## Findings
- **Transport works** = the same raw-McpServer stdio path that already runs today; wrapping it in `docker exec` is mechanically sound. No host Node needed — the runtime is the container.
- **Auth is the blocker for C4.** stdio resolves ONE token from the container's env (`getAuthToken`: per-request store → env, and there is no per-request store on stdio — @rekog guards are **HTTP-only**). So the container holds a single identity: `ot_sa` (machine tools work, `agent_conversation_*` 403) OR a human JWT (agent_conversation works but it expires in 24h and can't also be the durable machine identity). Cannot serve BOTH per-request like HTTP does → **C4 FAIL**.
- **Latency:** measured `docker exec <running container> true` ≈ **85–90ms** (×3: 91/87/84). That's the per-SESSION exec tax (stdio persists after connect, so it's not per-call) on top of in-container Node/MCP boot (~1–2s). `docker compose run --rm` is worse (container create/start each session).

## Rubric row — Spike B (docker-exec stdio)
- C1 no-host-Node: **PASS** (runs in container)
- C2 hybrid: **PARTIAL/FAIL** — requires a running mcp container; doesn't fit host-Nx-server hybrid cleanly
- C3 worktree-isolation: **PARTIAL** — per-worktree container name via OT_CONTAINER_PREFIX is feasible
- C4 agent_conv human-JWT: **FAIL** — stdio single-identity; no per-request header auth
- C5 latency: **PARTIAL** — ~85ms exec tax + Node boot per session (run --rm worse)
- C6 multi-client: **PARTIAL** — each client spawns its own exec/process (not a shared server)
- C7 hot-reload: **PARTIAL** — mount src + rebuild
- C8 config-simplicity: **PARTIAL** — `docker compose exec -T` args, container must be up first
- Verdict: viable for machine-only tools without host Node, but **fails the agent_conversation human-JWT criterion** — the same stdio ceiling as the status quo.

The runner now dumps each beat's visible text as it records (`output/<slug>/text/<beat>.txt`, and the portrait pass's equivalent), and the scanner checks those **plus the text that ships with the video** — the `.srt` and `metadata.json` — because a caption or a description leaks as easily as a frame.

Seven rules: `home-path`, `email-address`, `token-prefix` (sk-/ghp_/github_pat_/AKIA/xox), `jwt` and `denylist` fail the build; `high-entropy` and `external-url` warn.

**DOM text, not OCR.** The plan offered either. The DOM knows exactly what was rendered with no transcription errors and no dependency; `tesseract` is not installed on this host and adding it buys errors along with coverage. The gap is honest and written into the checklist as a human item: **the scan cannot see text baked into an image** — a screenshot inside the app, a logo, a chart label, a thumbnail.

**A false positive I had to design around, which is the interesting part.** The first run failed on `OpenThrottle/monorepo` — in `metadata.json`, where the standard description block is *supposed* to carry the repo URL. A rule that fires there trains everyone to ignore the scanner. So sources are now typed `frame` vs `shipped`, and the denylist applies to **frames only**: in a frame that same string means something far worse — the recording ran against the real database instead of the demo one, the worst failure this pipeline has. Also stopped URLs registering as high-entropy.
