## Task 1 findings — OpenRouter API surface + per-CLI reachability

Verified 2026-08-29 against the live service and the installed binaries. **No `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` is available on this host**, so everything auth-gated was probed with a deliberately invalid key: a `401 {"error":{"message":"User not found."}}` from openrouter.ai is treated as *proof the request reached OpenRouter and was correctly authenticated-and-rejected*, distinguished from a `404` control on a bogus path.

### (a) Catalog response shape — `GET https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models`

- **No auth required.** `http=200`, 640 KB, unauthenticated.
- Envelope: `{ data: [...], total_count, links }` — note `total_count` and `links` exist alongside `data`; the plan description only anticipated `{ data }`.
- **396 entries**, zero duplicate `id`s.
- Field coverage across all 396 (n = present):
  - Always present (396/396): `id`, `canonical_slug`, `name`, `description`, `created`, `context_length`, `architecture`, `pricing`, `top_provider`, `supported_parameters`, `default_parameters`, `per_request_limits`, `hugging_face_id`, `knowledge_cutoff`, `expiration_date`, `supported_voices`, `links`
  - **Optional** (must be tolerated as missing): `reasoning` (271/396), `benchmarks` (221/396), `alias_target` (12/396)
- `context_length` is an integer on 396/396; `name` non-empty on 396/396. Safe to require both, but keep the tolerant skip per the task spec.
- `architecture` = `{ modality: "text->text", input_modalities: [], output_modalities: [], tokenizer, instruct_type }`.
- `pricing` values are **decimal strings**, not numbers (`"0.000000834"`), and the key set varies (`prompt`, `completion`, `input_cache_read`, …).
- `reasoning` (when present) = `{ mandatory, default_enabled, supported_efforts: [...], default_effort }`.
- Ids are slugs: `anthropic/claude-opus-5`, `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5`, `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash`. Suffixed variants exist in the same list (`:free`, `:batch`) — task 2's de-dup must not collapse them, they are distinct routes.

### (b) Attribution headers

Per the API-reference overview: `HTTP-Referer` (site URL) and **`X-OpenRouter-Title`** as the canonical app-title header, with **`X-Title` documented as an accepted alias**. `X-OpenRouter-Categories` also exists. Task 3 should send `HTTP-Referer` + `X-OpenRouter-Title`; the quickstart's `X-Title` is not wrong, just the older spelling. Could not be A/B-tested live (needs a valid key) — this is documentation-sourced, flagged as such.

### Usage / cost — supersedes the task-9 premise

Per the usage-accounting docs: **`usage: { include: true }` and `stream_options: { include_usage: true }` are deprecated and have no effect — full usage is now always included in every response.** Task 9 must therefore *not* add `stream_options`. Returned `usage` carries `prompt_tokens`, `completion_tokens`, `total_tokens`, `cost`, `cost_details.upstream_inference_cost`, `prompt_tokens_details.{cached_tokens,cache_write_tokens,audio_tokens}`, `completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`. For streaming it arrives in the last SSE message.

### Reasoning effort

Not a global yes/no — it is **per model**, and the catalog already tells us: 133/396 models advertise `reasoning_effort` in `supported_parameters`, and `reasoning.supported_efforts` spans `minimal | none | low | medium | high | max | xhigh`. Task 4's capability descriptor should either drop the reasoning control (safest, since the advertised==honored contract is drift-guarded and OpenRouter's honoring varies by model) or derive it per-model from the catalog. Recommend **dropping it** for v1.

### Endpoint surface (401 = live, 404 control confirmed)

`POST /api/v1/{chat/completions, completions, responses, messages}` → all `401`. A bogus path → `404`. So OpenRouter serves **four** wire protocols, including an **Anthropic-compatible `/messages`** that returns an Anthropic-shaped error envelope. That is more than the plan assumed.

### Two traps found that change task 8

1. **`wire_api = "chat"` is REJECTED by codex 0.145.0 at config-load time** — `` `wire_api = "chat"` is no longer supported. How to fix: set `wire_api = "responses"` ``. # Task 5 — `openthrottle/no-adhoc-vocabulary`

## How it knows the vocabularies: neither (a) nor (b)

The task offered a static list in the rule's options or discovery of `vocabulary(...)` call sites,
and flagged the irony of (a). **Both were rejected; the rule matches syntax instead, so there is no
registry at all.**

- **(a) static list** — the rule policing hand-listed vocabularies, maintained as a hand-listed
  vocabulary. The irony is fatal, not decorative: that list drifts exactly like the ones it polices.
- **(b) discovery** — needs cross-file analysis. Confirmed the constraint the task asked me to
  verify: these rules run **without a type checker**, so a `Set` of `WorkspaceEditorId` members is
  indistinguishable by type from a `Set` of unrelated strings. Not tractable.

**(c)** the defect has a *syntactic* signature that needs neither. Two shapes:

1. `new Set([...])` containing ≥2 non-computed member accesses off a **single** object —
   `new Set<string>([Roles.a, Roles.b])`, the exact form that shipped the bug.
2. A module-scope **SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE** const whose initializer is an array of ≥2 such accesses —
   `[WorkspaceEditorId.Cursor, WorkspaceEditorId.Vscode]`. `as const` / `satisfies` are unwrapped
   first so an assertion cannot hide the list.

Requiring one shared object is what keeps `[Icons.Warning, Colors.Red]` out. Requiring SCREAMING_SNAKE
at module scope is what keeps inline JSX arrays out.

**SSOT files are skipped** — any file importing `@openthrottle/nodejs-parts-department`. That is the
one place members are supposed to appear.

## Two findings from building it, both worth keeping

**The bare-string half had to come out of the default.** I first flagged any literal `Set` of ≥2
string literals, reasoning that such a Set is "essentially always this defect." Running the rule on
its own project disproved that immediately: it fired on this file's own
`new Set<string>(['vocabulary', 'vocabularyFromEnum'])` — a plain lookup table, not a vocabulary
subset. A rule that cries wolf on its own source gets suppressed, which is precisely the failure the
task warned about. Bare-string lists (array *and* Set) are now behind
`includeStringLiteralArrays`, off by default, with a committed regression test pinning that. The
repo-wide survey of bare-string lists belongs to `scripts/audit-vocabularies.ts` (task 6), which
runs cross-file in node and *can* tell a union's members from arbitrary strings. Lint takes the
per-file certainties; the audit takes the survey.

**The SSOT check is an import check, not an AST walk.** My first version walked the AST generically
for `vocabulary(...)` calls, which required an `as` cast to re-enter the node union —
`@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-assertions` is `assertionStyle: 'never'` here, so it failed
typecheck. Checking `program.body` for an import of the package is type-safe, needs no recursion,
and is the more precise question anyway. Cost: a file importing the package only for its
`Vocabulary` *type* is also skipped — an acceptable false negative for a warn rule, since it only
ever suppresses, and only inside a file already wired to the machinery.

## The message teaches the fix

Both messages name `.subsetOf({...})`, state that **a subset must still be exhaustive**
(`Record<Member, boolean>`, so a new member forces an explicit yes or no rather than defaulting to
no), and the `adhocSet` message cites the shipped consequence — an editor that appeared checked in
the picker and was dropped on save.

## Shipped at `warn`, repo-wide

Registered as `openthrottle/no-adhoc-vocabulary` alongside the three sibling rules and wired
`'warn'`, matching the `route-primitive-shape` precedent. The comment records why, including the
PR #443 max-lines churn as the cautionary case.

**Invalid (6):** the verbatim pre-#443 `WORKSPACE_EDITOR_VALUES` Set; the pre-migration
`PROMPT_ROLES` Set; a bare-string Set under the option; the member-access array, bare and
`as const`; and the pre-migration `TERMINAL_TASK_STATUSES` under the option.

**Valid (14).** The real migrated call sites from tasks 3, 4 and 4.5 all stay silent — both SSOT
declarations, the migrated `PROMPT_ROLES`, `TERMINAL_TASK_STATUSES`, `WORKSPACE_EDITOR_OPTIONS`, and

Task 3 — guard shipped, but with the error/warn split INVERTED from the spec, because the spec'd version cannot be turned on.

The task asked to fail when `exports` resolves into a gitignored build dir while `main` resolves into `src/`, and to merely warn when the package also self-imports. I built exactly that first and it flagged **39 of 70** workspace packages. `import` → `dist` with `main` → `src` is the workspace *norm*, not the defect: consumers get the package built through Nx `^build`, so it is harmless. Gating on it would demand a 39-package migration this plan never scoped, and would block every PR on day one.

What actually breaks is the *combination* — the mis-pointed condition plus the package's own `src/**` importing itself by name — because a project's `test` target depends on `^build` (dependencies) and never on its own `build`. So the two conditions are swapped:

- **error**: Vite-resolved condition (`import`, or a bare/`default` string) lands in a gitignored dir AND the package's own `src/` imports it by name. Exactly the task-1 failure.
- **warn**: the same mis-pointed condition with no self-import — latent, arms itself the moment someone writes an entry test.

`scripts/check-package-entrypoints.ts`:
- Walks `applications/`, `packages/`, `tools/`; flattens each `exports` map to one entry per declared string target, tracking subpath and condition.
- Ignored-ness comes from `git check-ignore --stdin` — the real `.gitignore`, per the task's requirement, so a package that commits its build output is not flagged.
- Self-import detection is `git grep -q --fixed-strings "from '<name>'"` scoped to the package's own `src/`.
- 39 latent packages would be 82 warning lines on every run, so warnings collapse to one summary line; `--verbose` lists them.

Wiring:
- `nx.json` targetDefault `check-package-entrypoints` with explicit `{workspaceRoot}` inputs — required, since the root `monorepo` project owns zero files and the default `{projectRoot}` input would hash nothing and cache-hit forever (same trap already documented on `check-agent-assets-ssot`).
- `.github/workflows/continuous-integration.yml`: new `📦 Package entrypoint consistency` step gated to `matrix.jobIndex == 1`, alongside the agent-assets cluster. Static and build-free, so one shard is enough.
- `package.json`: `check:local:package-entrypoints`, chained into `check:local` between the migration-comments and rbac-coverage gates.

## Task 1 — CI step-timing baseline (ubuntu-latest, post-6ced8d0e)

Sampled `build` jobs via `gh api .../actions/runs/<id>/jobs`. Only runs AFTER the free-runner
migration count (earlier runs are Blacksmith + GCS remote cache and are not comparable).

| run | event | outcome | setup* | codegen | lint+typecheck | test | once-per-run gates | job total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32181320967 | PR (fat) | success | 56s | 27s | 4m14s | 10m51s | 20s | **17m07s** |
| 32177010511 | PR (fat) | success | 56s | 24s | (17m50s combined) | | 21s | **19m45s** |
| 32181037247 | push main (full graph) | failure | 43s | 31s | (27m01s combined) | | skipped | **28m24s** |
| 32173900260 | PR | cancelled | 45s | 31s | (28m55s, cancelled) | | skipped | 30m18s |

\* setup = `Set up job` + checkout (`blob:none`, depth 0) + `Node Setup` (pnpm install + Actions
Nx cache restore) + skill-sync symlinks + nx-set-shas.

Blacksmith reference for contrast (thin affected sets, GCS cache): affected step 3m49s / 7m26s.

### What the numbers say

- **Per-box fixed overhead ≈ 1.6 min** (85s setup+codegen, ~12s post). That is 6% of a typical
  17 min job and 9% of the 28 min worst case. Setup is NOT the bottleneck.
- **Shardable work is 88–95% of the job.** `test` alone is 10m51s of a 17m07s job; the heavy
  affected graph on `main` pushed the combined affected step to 27m01s — 90% of the 30 m
  `timeout-minutes` ceiling, and one run was cancelled at 28m55s inside that step. The ceiling
  is already the live risk, not a future one.
- **The heaviest single project does not bind.** Per-suite Vitest durations in run 32181320967:
  195s, 181s, 155s, 152s, ~196s (5 heavy app suites), then a long tail of 1–24s package suites.
  Worst single project ≈ 195s test + its lint/typecheck ≈ 4 min, so a shard floor of
  ~1.6 + 4 ≈ 5.6 min sits well under the N=3 ideal split.

### Decision: N = 3 project shards, single `target: ['lint,typecheck,test']`

Projected worst case (28 min baseline): N=2 → 1.6 + 27/2 ≈ **15.1 min**; N=3 → 1.6 + 27/3 ≈
**10.6 min**. Typical (17 min baseline): N=3 ≈ **7.6 min**.

- N=3 over N=2 because the extra box costs $0 on this public repo and N=2 still leaves the worst
  case at half the ceiling. The 1.6 min setup tax buys nothing back at N=2 that it doesn't at N=3.
- Not 3 because it "looks even": 3 is where worst case clears the ceiling with real margin
  (10.6 of 30) while staying above the ~5.6 min single-project floor. A 4th box would start
  paying overhead for shards below that floor.
- **Target-split fallback NOT taken.** It is the right call only if project shards are
  setup-bound; measurement says setup is 6–9%, so it is not. Target-split would also leave the
  10m51s test graph whole on one box, which is precisely the segment that is growing.
- Stays on `ubuntu-latest`. No Nx Cloud, no managed/larger runners.

### Risk to watch in task 6

`nx affected --exclude=…` per shard re-materializes each chunk's *dependency* tasks (run
32181320967: "22 projects and 87 tasks they depend on"), so build deps are partly duplicated
across boxes. The Actions cache restore should absorb most of it, and the 10.6 vs 28 min gap
leaves wide headroom — but measure it rather than assume, and watch for shard imbalance since
the partition is round-robin by name, not duration-weighted. Apps-first round-robin does spread
the 5 heavy app suites across the 3 shards, which is the behaviour we want.

# Task 3 — GraphQL exposure

## Where it hangs: a sibling query, not a field on `workspaceSettings`

`editorPresence` is its own top-level query in its own module (`graphql/editor-presence/`), registered independently in `app.module.ts`.

Presence is a nicety; the editor preferences it annotates are not. Hanging it off the `workspaceSettings` payload would couple the two failure modes in both directions — a probe problem could take down the settings page it only decorates. As a separate query the client fetches it in its own document and renders no hints when it fails. Same reasoning the plan-detail route landed on.

Guard is `PERMISSIONS.SETTINGS_READ`, matching `workspaceSettings`. No new permission.

## Two bugs the work surfaced

1. **`private readonly editorPresence` shadowed the resolver method.** A constructor property with the query's name overwrites the prototype method on the instance, so `resolver.editorPresence` was the service, not the query — `TypeError: not a function` in all four resolver tests. Field renamed to `presence`, with a comment so nobody reintroduces it.
2. **The module was missing `NestjsRepositoriesModule`.** `GqlPermissionsGuard` injects `RolesService`; without it the whole server failed to bootstrap (`UnknownDependenciesException`). Caught only by actually booting for the schema regen — no unit test would have, since the resolver test overrides the guard.

## Task 1 decision — how a created skill becomes discoverable

**Decision: Option A — the action runs `sync.sh`.** One narrowly-scoped `.server.ts` module, `execFileSync`, fixed argv.

### Verified, not assumed

- **`child_process` really is absent.** `grep -rn "child_process|execSync|spawnSync|execFileSync|execa" applications/openthrottle-developer/app` → zero hits. This module is the app's first subprocess.
- **Discovery never sees either destination.** `discover-repo-skills.server.ts` `LAYOUT_SCAN_TARGETS` is exactly `.agents/skills`, `.claude/skills`, `.codex/skills`, `.cursor/skills`, `.grok/skills`, `.opencode/skills`. Neither `skills/` nor the personal root is scanned. A write-only action produces a file that never appears on `/skills` — confirming the premise.
- **Both destinations need the same sync.** `sync.sh` stage 1 links `skills/<name>` and stage 1b links `<personal>/<name>`, both into `.agents/skills/`, then stage 2 fans out. One `sync.sh` call covers both — no per-destination branching in the sync step.

### `personal.sh new` — read, and NOT reusable for the write

`command_new` = `assert_valid_slug` → `assert_name_is_free` → `write_template` → `bash sync.sh`. It **does** scaffold + sync in one step, but `write_template` emits a *fixed* `TODO —` heredoc. It has no way to accept editor-authored content, and there is no flag to supply it. Shelling out to it would write the wrong file and then need overwriting — worse than writing the file ourselves.

What *is* reusable is its **rule set**, which task 2 mirrors in TS rather than invokes:
- `assert_valid_slug` — kebab-case, no leading/trailing/doubled hyphen (`AGENT_ASSET_SLUG_PATTERN`)
- `assert_name_is_free` — collision against `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, against `lockfile_skill_names` (`skills-lock.json`), and against `<personal>/<name>`

Its wording is deliberately identical to sync's; task 2's copy should match that phrasing for the same reason.

### The personal-root precedence is already shared — do not re-derive it

`resolvePersonalSkillsRoot` (`packages/openthrottle-agentic-utils`, `personal-skills-config.ts`) is `OPENTHROTTLE_PERSONAL_SKILLS_DIR` (trimmed, non-empty) → `join(homedir(), '.openthrottle', 'skills')`. `common.sh`'s `resolve_personal_skills_root` is the same precedence. Task 2 imports the TS one — it is what `skill-path-allowlist.server.ts` already uses, so module and sync agree by construction.

### Guard list the module will carry (Option A specifics)

Before any subprocess:
1. `getMonorepoRoot()` null ⇒ refuse, no spawn (mirrors the edit path's deployed-app refusal).
2. Script path is built as `join(monorepoRoot, 'skills/ot-skill-sync/scripts/sync.sh')` — a **constant** relative path, never client input — and must exist and pass realpath containment inside `monorepoRoot`.

The spawn itself:
3. `execFileSync('bash', [scriptPath])` — array argv, no shell, so no interpolation surface. **No user-derived value ever enters argv**; the slug reaches sync only as a directory already on disk.
4. `cwd` pinned to `monorepoRoot`. Load-bearing: `detect_repo_root()` is `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`, so cwd decides which repo gets synced.

6. Env: inherit, explicitly preserving `OPENTHROTTLE_PERSONAL_SKILLS_DIR` so sync resolves the same personal root the module just wrote into. A mismatch here is the subtle failure — module writes to root X, sync links root Y, skill never appears.

## Task 3 (d4d987ab) — partitioner audit: **the fix IS needed, but not for the reason the brief assumed**

### Key mechanic the brief did not capture

`getAffectedProjects()` ends with `[...affected].sort()` — the affected list is **alphabetically sorted** before partitioning. That makes the partition fully deterministic and exactly simulatable. Workspace shape: **72 projects, 8 non-`@` ("applications"), 64 `@`-prefixed ("packages"), `jobCount: 3`.**

Crucially, alphabetical sort puts **every `@…` name before every non-`@` name**. That interacts badly with the naive fix, below.

### 1-2. Simulated partitions — no collision in any *concrete* scenario

Faithful port of `distributeEvenly()`, post-split project list (74 projects):

| scenario | affected | dev shard | routing shard | kernel shard | collision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S1 full-affected (`main` push) | 74 | 1 | 3 | 2 | **no** |
| S2 app-only (`routes/**`) | 2 | 2 | — | — | n/a |
| S3 routing-only | 3 | 2 | 3 | — | **no** |
| S4 app + kernel + routing | 4 | 2 | 1 | 3 | **no** |

Full-affected detail: 8 apps dealt first, `developer-routing` is `packages[3]`, so its chunk is `(8 + 3) % 3 = 2` → shard 3, while `openthrottle-developer` is `apps[3]` → chunk 0 → shard 1. It also survives a **single-project sensitivity sweep**: removing any one of the other 72 projects never induces a collision from that baseline.

### The real finding: it is lucky, not safe — **30% collision across realistic affected sets**

Collision occurs iff `dev_index ≡ n_affected_apps + routing_index (mod 3)`. All three quantities vary per run, so the concrete scenarios above are three lucky draws, not a property.

Monte-Carlo over 20,000 realistic affected sets (developer + routing always affected, other apps/packages varied):

```
current partitioner : 6009/20000 collide = 30.0%
```

Essentially 1-in-3, as the modular arithmetic predicts. **Since most CI runs are partial-affected PR pushes, roughly one PR in three would place both heavy units on one box and erase the entire Phase B win on that run.** Against a best-case ceiling of ~22%, that is not an acceptable expected value.

### 3. The fix — and a **failed first attempt worth recording**

**Attempt 1 (the brief's suggestion): explicit heavy allowlist dealt in the applications pass. THIS DOES NOT WORK.**

```
WITH heavy-allowlist fix : 5032/20000 collide = 25.2%
```

30% → 25% only. Cause: `@openthrottle/developer-routing` still sorts **before** every non-`@` app name, so it becomes `heavy[0]` while `openthrottle-developer` sits several positions later. The gap between them still varies with the affected-app count, so the modular collision survives. Anyone implementing the obvious version of this fix will think it worked — it does not.

**Attempt 2 (recommended): deal an ORDERED heaviest-first list before everything else.**

```js
// The two heaviest units are dealt FIRST and ADJACENTLY, in this fixed order, so
// round-robin necessarily puts them on different boxes. Order matters: sorting
// alone will not do it, because `@…` names sort ahead of application names.
const HEAVY_ORDER = ['@openthrottle/developer-routing', 'openthrottle-developer'];
```
Deal `HEAVY_ORDER` (filtered to the affected set) first, then remaining applications, then remaining packages.

```
ordered-heavy : 0/20000 collide = 0.0%
```

**Structurally guaranteed, not statistical** — two adjacent deals always land on consecutive chunks whenever `chunkCount >= 2`. Full-affected and app+routing-only both give routing→shard 1, dev→shard 2.

### 4. Round-trip check — no change needed

`getShardSelectionErrors()` is name-agnostic (pure set comparison) and needs no modification. `@`-prefixed names already work in `--exclude` selectors — all 64 existing packages depend on it, verified directly. Direct project names only; the `!tag:name:` trap in the header is not engaged by this change.

### Verdict

**Phase B is not worth doing until `parallelize-tasks.ts` gets the ordered-heavy-first deal.** The change is ~6 lines plus a header comment, fits the script's existing style, and is independently harmless — it can land before or with Phase B. Without it, ~30% of PR runs get zero benefit from a 1,255-file refactor.

This tightens rather than resolves the gate: the ceiling is still ~22%, and now there is a mandatory prerequisite change attached to realising it.

## Baseline task (41133fc7) — measurements: **Phase B loses decisively to a config-only alternative**

> Measured locally in the worktree, deps warm, app target forced cold by touching `app/global/config/settings.ts`. Absolute times are faster than a 4-vCPU CI runner; the **ratios** are what transfer, and the ratios are lopsided enough that runner speed does not change the conclusion.

### 1. Pre-split baseline — heaviest unit (`openthrottle-developer`)

| target | wall clock | share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| lint | 9.6s | 5.5% |
| typecheck | 10.6s | 6.1% |
| **test** | **154.1s** | **88.4%** |
| **total** | **174.3s** | |

**`test` is 88% of the heaviest unit.** `lint` + `typecheck` together are 20.2s — **11.6%**.

### 2. What Vitest `--shard` buys, config-only

Ran `nx run openthrottle-developer:test -- --shard=N/3`. Works out of the box, no code movement, all shards green:

| shard | test files | wall clock |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1/3 | 227 | **60.9s** |
| 2/3 | 226 | 54.6s |
| 3/3 | 226 | 48.4s |

Heaviest shard **60.9s vs 154.1s → a 60% cut to the test slice.**

### 3. Head-to-head on the heaviest unit

| option | heaviest-unit wall clock | reduction | cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| baseline today | 174.3s | — | — |
| **Vitest `--shard` 3-way** | **81.1s** (60.9 test + 9.6 lint + 10.6 typecheck) | **−53%** | config + workflow only, **zero files moved** |
| **Phase B split** | **~134s** (~120s test at 529/679 files + ~14s lint/typecheck) | **−23%** | **1,255 files moved, 325 import sites rewritten**, plus the mandatory partitioner fix |
| both combined | ~62s | −64% | everything above |

**Vitest `--shard` alone delivers more than twice Phase B's improvement, for a config-only change.** Phase B on top of it adds ~19s more on the heaviest unit — for the entire 1,255-file refactor.

And Phase B's −23% is the *optimistic* figure: without task d4d987ab's ordered-heavy-first partitioner fix, ~30% of PR runs collide and get **0%**.

### 4. Why this was missed — and it is not an oversight in the plan

`applications/openthrottle-developer/vitest.config.ts` already reasons about exactly this, and concludes:

> "project sharding splits the affected PROJECT list, and this suite is a single Nx project, so whichever box draws it runs all of it. **The matrix cannot lower this suite's wall-clock — a faster pool can.**"

That is **correct about project sharding and the reason the vmForks work happened** (forks 253s -> vmForks 86s, plan `e448a51d`). But it treats "faster pool" and "move the code" as the only two levers. **Vitest's own `--shard` is a third lever** — it splits *within* a project, needs no code movement, and the numbers above show it works on this suite today. The CI workflow comment at line 225 likewise calls the heaviest project a hard "floor… which suite sharding cannot split"; that floor is not actually hard.

Related: plan `e448a51d` (Developer Vitest sharding, DONE, PR #267 unmerged) is in this same territory and should be reconciled with this finding.

### Verdict handed to the owner

**Recommend NO-GO on Phase B as a CI-time play.** Its stated justification is heaviest-shard wall-clock, and on that measure it is beaten roughly 2.3x by a config-only change that is already available.

This is *not* an argument that Phase B is worthless — the structural payoff is real (the ~60 cross-domain `routing/X -> routing/Y` edges becoming intra-library, and a cleaner starting point for `653d1be5`). But that is an **architecture** justification, not the CI-time one this plan was written on, and it should be argued and prioritised on those terms rather than on a 23% number that a config change beats.

## Task 3 — session-id parsing, re-scoped per the task 1 evidence

The task was written to fix hypothesis 1 ("a banner poisons the id and `--resume <garbage>` fails"). Task 1 disproved that premise: `--resume` **accepts any string**, including `"Update available!  1.2.3"`, and returns a fully successful turn.

So the work landed with the same shape but an honest rationale: a polluted id does not *fail*, it silently starts a **fresh, disconnected chat** and echoes the junk back as `session_id`. The conversation loses every prior turn while every surface reports success. Validating at the mint is the only place that failure is visible — which makes this worth landing even though it is not the cold-start fix.

`cursor-agent/session-id.ts` — `parseCursorChatId(stdout): string | null`:

- strips a leading BOM and ANSI/VT escapes (CSI, OSC, single-char), then splits on LF/CRLF into trimmed non-empty lines
- **two tiers.** Prefers a canonical UUID anywhere in the output — the shape cursor mints today, confirmed from `handleCreateChat` calling `crypto.randomUUID()` and from 10 observed captures. Only if no UUID is present does it fall back to a conservative single-token rule (`[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._:-]{7,127}`), so a future cursor release that changes the format degrades instead of hard-failing. Per the task's warning, the strict UUID check is a preference, not the only gate.
- **last match wins** within each tier, since banners print first
- returns `null` rather than junk; `createCursorAgentSession()` turns that into a throw carrying the captured stdout (via task 2's `formatCursorMintFailure`)

Note the tiering is load-bearing: a plain preference for the last matching line would pick `some.other.token.value` over a real UUID printed above it. Covered by a test.

## Task 1 — Spike findings (zod/v3 compat on zod@4.4.3)

### Issue-code inventory (what parseFormData actually emits)
| Case | code | key fields | default message |
|---|---|---|---|
| missing required (string/enum/number) | `invalid_type` | `received:'undefined'`, `expected` | `Required` |
| empty string → `.min(1)` | `too_small` | `minimum:1`, `type:'string'` | `String must contain at least 1 character(s)` |
| wrong scalar type (number into string) | `invalid_type` | `received:'number'` | `Expected string, received number` |
| bad enum value | `invalid_enum_value` | `options:[...]`, `received` | `Invalid enum value…` |
| bad number string | `invalid_type` | `received:'string'` | `Expected number, received string` |
| nested path | any | `path:['input','tag']` | — |

Note: in practice a blank form field is trimmed→dropped by `normalizeScalar`, so the common "required" path is `invalid_type received:'undefined'`, NOT `too_small`. The `too_small` path only fires when a genuinely non-empty-then-empty value or `lists` collapse reaches `.min(1)`.

### errorMap precedence (the important finding)
**Zod does NOT invoke the parse-level `errorMap` for any issue that already carries an explicit author message.** Confirmed:
- `.min(1, 'AUTHOR:custom')` on empty → `AUTHOR:custom` (map's `too_small` handler never ran).
- `.refine(fn, 'AUTHOR:refine')` on bad value → `AUTHOR:refine`.

⇒ **No "did the author supply a message" detection is needed.** The map only ever sees default-message issues, so it can rewrite freely and authored messages win untouched.

Caveat: the `z.string({ required_error })` / `invalid_type_error` *sugar* does NOT win over a parse-level errorMap in this v4 compat shim (map won). This is acceptable — generated schemas use bare `.min(1)` with no args, and the issue-level string form (`.min(1,'x')`, `.refine`) — the form actually used for bespoke copy — works correctly.

### Decisions (also written to plan description)
- **Label rule:** last path segment → split camelCase + snake_case into words → sentence case (capitalize first word only). `startIso`→"Start iso", `project_id`→"Project id", `tag`→"Tag".
- **too_small (string):** `minimum===1` → "{Label} is required."; `minimum>1` → "{Label} must be at least {n} characters."; else `ctx.defaultError`.
- **Override shape:** `ParseFormDataOptions.labels?: Record<path,string>` (swap the humanized label, message template kept) AND `messages?: Record<path,string>` (replace the whole message for a path; wins over labels). Both keyed by dot-joined path.
- No codegen changes. Single-file central errorMap.

## Task 2 (0930f67f) — nested `project.json` shortcut: **DISPROVEN, decisively**

The shortcut does not work. It fails green, which is the worst way to fail. Do not re-propose it.

### Context worth knowing first

**No `project.json` exists anywhere in this repo.** Every project is declared via the `nx` field in its `package.json`, with targets plugin-inferred (`openthrottle-developer`'s `test` target is literally `{}`). So the nested-project idea was not just untested here — it is foreign to how the workspace declares projects at all.

Probe used: minimal `project.json` at `app/routing/schedule` (smallest domain — 26 files, 11 test files), named `developer-routing-schedule-probe`, explicit `lint`/`test`/`typecheck` targets, **every `~/...` import left untouched**.

### 2. Nx records NO edge — confirmed

Nx *does* register it as a project (74 total, up from 73). But:

```
openthrottle-developer -> developer-routing-schedule-probe : NONE
anyone                 -> developer-routing-schedule-probe : NOBODY
```

Nothing in the workspace depends on it. Meanwhile the nested project *does* resolve its own outgoing edges to real package names:

```
developer-routing-schedule-probe -> @openthrottle/react-router-shadcn, react-router-markdown,
                                    react-router-ui, react-router-ui-global, react-router-chat
```

That asymmetry is the whole story: **real package specifiers create edges, `~/*` path aliases do not.** Nx's import analysis resolves `~/*` through the app's own tsconfig `paths` and never leaves the app.

Correction to an earlier reading: a clean control (graph with vs. without the `project.json`, same install state) shows the app's dependency **list is unchanged — 25 deps either way, nothing lost, nothing gained**. An apparent loss of `openthrottle-email` was an artifact of comparing against the task-1 probe-era graph. The damage is not in the dep list; it is in the input hashing, below.

### 3. The false cache hit — CONFIRMED, and it reports GREEN

Controlled experiment. Only one variable changes: whether `project.json` exists. The edit (`app/routing/schedule/utils/format-duration.ts`, a source file the app's own suite executes) is **identical and still in place** across both rows.

| condition | app `test` outcome | wall clock |
| --- | --- | --- |
| warm baseline, `project.json` present | 679 files ran, pass | 164s |
| **`project.json` present + source file edited** | **`17 out of 17 tasks` cached — "Successfully ran target test"** | **1.3s** |
| **`project.json` REMOVED, same edit still in place** | **re-executed, 679 files** | **155s** |

**Nx reported success, from cache, on stale inputs.** The app still *runs* those 11 schedule test files when it executes (vitest globs the directory regardless of Nx project boundaries) — but Nx no longer counts them as inputs, so it never knows it should execute. CI would go green on unbuilt, untested changes.

### 4. Second problem, same root cause

The file-set exclusion is what causes the above: Nx removes nested-project files from the parent's file set for hashing purposes, while the parent's *test runner* still picks them up. Declaring the project changes what Nx hashes without changing what vitest runs — the two disagree, silently, in the unsafe direction.

### Verdict

**Justifies the real extraction.** You cannot get a working Nx boundary by declaring a project in place; the imports have to become real package specifiers, which means the code has to move. Task 1 proved the moved-code version works correctly; this task proves the cheap version is actively dangerous.

Tree reverted, `project.json` deleted, workspace clean.

## ⚠️ This test found a SEPARATE, more serious bug

Writing it, the "editors first" case failed while "skills first" passed. That order-dependence was the tell, and it is not a test artifact.

**Applying editor configuration causes foreign-skill injection to silently drop 10 of OT's own curated skills.**

`applyForRepositoryEditor` does `mkdir(dirname(...))` for every entry in `OPENTHROTTLE_REPO_SKILL_PATHS`, creating **empty** `.agents/skills/<slug>/` directories for: `brag-sheet`, `git-commit`, `link-workspace-packages`, `monitor-ci`, `nx-workspace`, `ot-claude-loop`, `ot-generators`, `ot-plans`, `ot-stack`, `workflow-ralph`.

`scanTargetOwnedSkillNames` then reads those directories, treats each name as one **the target repo owns**, and the resolver drops it from the manifest before materialization — the target-wins rule from design doc §1 doing exactly what it was designed to do, against directories OT created itself.

Reproduced directly, outside the test:

```
editor-config applied first = false
  injected: [ 'nx-workspace', 'ot-plans', 'some-other-skill' ]
  ot-plans really present? true

editor-config applied first = true
  injected: [ 'some-other-skill' ]
  ot-plans really present? false        <- empty directory, no SKILL.md
```

So a user who applies editor config to a foreign repo ends up with **empty directories where OT's skills should be**. Worse than the residue this plan fixes: the residue was cosmetic, this is missing functionality that looks present on disk.

Entirely pre-existing — neither this plan nor `b409da6e` introduced it. Both orders are reachable in the real product: the editor apply and injection are independent user actions.

Fixing it needs a decision this plan should not make (should the apply create those dirs at all? should injection ignore an empty dir? should OT-created dirs be recorded so injection can tell them apart?), so it is **filed separately** rather than absorbed here.

## Task 1 — Spike results (Nx 22.7.4): workspaceChangelog under independent projects

**Bottom line: the plan's chosen mechanism is NOT achievable in-scope. Nx hard-disables the workspace changelog whenever projects are `independent`, and the two workarounds the plan hypothesized (explicit `--version`; `renderOptions`/`versionTitleDate`) do NOT bypass it — the early-return happens before version or render logic runs.**

### Commands run (worktree, --dry-run only, no nx.json edits)
- `pnpm nx release changelog --dry-run --first-release`
  → `An explicit target version must be specified when using the changelog command directly` (independent projects → `nx release changelog` needs a positional `version`).
- `pnpm nx release changelog 0.0.0 --dry-run --first-release`
  → `NX  Release group "__default__" matches no projects.` (see Blocker #1)
- Same with `-p <project>` / `--printConfig` → identical "matches no projects" error. The nx.json `release.projects` group filter is applied first; `-p`/`--projects` cannot widen past an empty group.

### Blocker #1 — release group matches ZERO projects
`nx.json` `release.projects: ["tag:publish:true", "!tag:production:false"]`. Grep of every project.json/package.json: **69 projects tagged `publish:false`, none tagged `publish:true`.** No `*@*` release tags exist either. So `nx release` (any subcommand) errors immediately before any changelog work — the existing config, including the "per-project changelogs create GitHub releases" described in the plan, is currently never exercised.

### Blocker #2 — Nx disables workspaceChangelog under `projectsRelationship: "independent"` (hard-coded)
Source: `nx/dist/src/command-line/release/changelog.js` → `generateChangelogForWorkspace()`:
```js
if (Object.entries(nxReleaseConfig.groups).length > 1) { output.warn(...); return; }
if (Object.values(nxReleaseConfig.groups)[0].projectsRelationship === 'independent') {
  output.warn({ title: `Workspace changelog is enabled, but you have configured an independent projects relationship. This is not supported, so workspace changelog will be disabled.` });
  return;   // <-- returns BEFORE reading config.file, renderOptions, or workspaceChangelogVersion
}
```
So workspaceChangelog is only ever generated when there is **exactly one** release group AND that group is **`fixed`**. Passing `--version` doesn't help (the return precedes `ReleaseVersion`/render). `renderOptions`/`versionTitleDate` don't help (never reached).

### Explicit answer to the spike question ("how is the workspace entry title produced under independent projects?")
It isn't. Under independent projects Nx skips workspace-changelog generation entirely (warn + early return). Title derivation (`new ReleaseVersion({version: workspaceChangelogVersion, ...})`) is dead code in this configuration.

### Config shape (for reference; confirmed valid but moot here)
`NxReleaseChangelogConfiguration` (nx-json.d.ts:213): `workspaceChangelog?: NxReleaseChangelogConfiguration | boolean`, fields `createRelease`, `file` (`"{workspaceRoot}/CHANGELOG.md"` default), `entryWhenNoChanges`, `renderer`, `renderOptions` (`DefaultChangelogRenderOptions`: `authors`, `applyUsernameToAuthors`, `commitReferences`, `versionTitleDate`). All valid — but the independent-group guard makes them irrelevant.

### Consequence for tasks 2–5
Flipping `workspaceChangelog` to an object (Task 2) would emit the "not supported… will be disabled" warning and produce **no** root CHANGELOG (Task 3 verification would fail). The only native fixes are explicitly **out of scope**: (a) switch to a single `fixed`/unified group, or (b) custom git-cliff/conventional-changelog tooling. → Surfacing to the plan author for a decision before touching nx.json.

# Task 1 — Spike decision: automatic outcome-capture mechanism

## Chosen mechanism: `Stop` hook + session-scoped start-correlation store

Wire a new completion hook under Claude Code's **`Stop`** event. On each fire it reads the
open skill-starts recorded for that `session_id` (the correlation store built in task 2),
emits one `recordSkillUsageOutcome` per open start with `duration_ms = stopTime − started_at`,
then drains those starts. This is **additive** — the `PreToolUse:Skill` / `UserPromptExpansion`
capture path is untouched and remains the system of record for the Invocations column.

## Alternatives considered & rejected
- **`PostToolUse:Skill`** — rejected as the primary signal. The Skill tool returns as soon as
  the skill's instructions are loaded into the turn; for **inline** skills (ot-plans, git-commit,
  most authored skills) the actual work then interleaves with the rest of the turn, so
  PostToolUse fires near-instantly → a ~0ms, meaningless duration. It is only accurate for
  subagent-backed skills (where the Skill call blocks on the subagent). Not worth a second
  code path for that minority in v1.
- **`SubagentStop`** — considered, deferred. Its payload carries `session_id` but **no**
  `tool_use_id`/`skill_name`/per-subagent id we can rely on, so resolving "all open starts for
  the session" at a SubagentStop would prematurely close *main-agent* inline starts recorded
  before the subagent ran. Precise correlation needs per-agent start scoping we don't have yet.
  Subagent-invoked skill starts still get closed at the next main-agent `Stop` (duration then
  spans the subagent run — an accepted approximation). Documented as a future refinement.
- **Keep manual opt-in only (roll helper into every SKILL.md)** — rejected as the goal is
  "zero manual steps." The manual helper is retained as an **opt-in precision** path.

## Harness payload shape (confirmed for the wired events)
All Claude Code hooks receive JSON on stdin with common fields: `session_id`,
`transcript_path`, `cwd`, `hook_event_name`.
- **`Stop`** (and `SubagentStop`): add `stop_hook_active` (bool, loop-guard). **No**
  `tool_use_id`, `skill_name`, or reliable per-turn error field. → correlation is
  **session-scoped only** (`session_id`); the skill identity comes from the start store, not
  the Stop payload.
- **`PreToolUse:Skill`** (existing capture): carries `session_id`, `tool_use_id`,
  `tool_input.skill`, optional `agent_id`/`agent_type` — enough to record a start row.

## Outcome-inference rules
- **success** — default for any start resolved by a `Stop`. (The turn completed normally.)
- **abandoned** — a start that is never resolved because its session ended without a `Stop`
  (e.g. session killed mid-turn). Swept opportunistically: start-files belonging to a session
  other than the current one, older than a staleness threshold, are emitted as `abandoned`
  with `duration_ms = null`, then drained.
- **error** — NOT reliably inferable from the `Stop` payload (no error field). v1's automatic
  path emits **success**; `error` stays reachable via the manual opt-in helper

**Third finding — scheduled runs cannot record token cost or spend.**

`ScheduledAgentJobsProcessor.foldRunUsage` parses a run's buffered output as JSONL to populate `costUsd` / `inputTokens` / `outputTokens` / `totalTokens` / `rawUsage` on the run row. The processor's own comment ("opencode emits several mid-stream usage lines") suggests this was written against drivers that do emit JSONL; `claude` does not.

## Task 2 — Spike: `--shard` through the @nx/vitest executor and Nx hashing

All runs on the worktree `loop-plan-developer-vitest-shard`, `CI=true`, local 10-core box.

### Q1 — Does the undeclared `--shard` flag survive the executor? **YES.**

```
CI=true pnpm exec nx run openthrottle-developer:test --shard=1/3 --skip-nx-cache
  → Test Files  227 passed (227)   Duration 45.88s
CI=true pnpm exec nx run openthrottle-developer:test --shard=2/3
  → Test Files  226 passed (226)   Duration 43.81s
CI=true pnpm exec nx run openthrottle-developer:test --shard=3/3 --skip-nx-cache
  → Test Files  226 passed (226)   Duration 43.56s
CI=true pnpm exec nx run openthrottle-developer:test --skip-nx-cache
  → Test Files  679 passed (679)   Duration 136.94s
```

**227 + 226 + 226 = 679.** The shards partition the suite exactly; nothing is double-run and nothing is dropped. This is the "silently-ignored flag" check the task asked for — a dropped flag would have shown 679 files three times.

Why it works, from the source rather than by luck: `nx.json`'s `targetDefaults.test.options` already carries `passWithNoTests`, which is **also** undeclared in `node_modules/@nx/vitest/src/executors/test/schema.json` — Nx does not strip options absent from the schema. The executor's `getOptions()` (`.../executors/test/lib/utils.js`) then does `parseCLI(['vitest', ...getOptionsAsArgv(options)])`, i.e. it re-serialises the whole option bag to argv and hands it to **Vitest's own CLI parser**, which normalises `--shard=1/3` into `{ shard: { index: 1, count: 3 } }`. Everything not explicitly destructured falls into `passThroughOptions` and is spread into the config handed to `startVitest()`. So `--shard` reaches Vitest by the documented passthrough path, not by an accident of arg forwarding.

**No fallback needed.** Options (a) `--` passthrough, (b) three explicit `test-shard-*` targets, (c) an `nx:run-commands` Vitest-CLI target, (d) an env-driven shard read inside `vitest.config.ts` are all unnecessary. Recording why (d) would have been the *worst* of them even though it looks tidiest: a shard read from `process.env` inside the config is invisible to Nx's task hash, which is exactly the Q3 failure mode below, deliberately engineered in.

### Q3 — Does the Nx cache distinguish the shards? **YES.** (highest-risk item, demonstrated)

```
# shard 2/3 immediately after shard 1/3 had populated the cache:
  → ran fresh, 226 files, "read the output from the cache for 16 out of 17 tasks"
    (the 16 are the codegen/build dependencies; the test task itself RAN)

# shard 2/3 again, unchanged:
  → "read the output from the cache for 17 out of 17 tasks", replayed the
    identical earlier output (same `Start at 20:10:22` timestamp)
```

Both directions demonstrated: a *different* shard is a cache **miss**, the *same* shard is a cache **hit**. CLI overrides participate in the task hash, so boxes 2 and 3 cannot replay box 1's result. This was the plan's single highest-risk failure mode and it does not exist on this invocation shape.

### Bonus — `run-many` carries the flag identically

```
CI=true pnpm exec nx run-many --projects=openthrottle-developer --target=test --shard=1/3
  → 17 of 17 cached; replayed the `nx run openthrottle-developer:test --shard=1/3` result verbatim
```

A full cache hit against the `nx run …` form proves `run-many` produces the *same task hash*, not merely a similar command. Either invocation shape is safe; task 3/4 will use `run-many --projects=…` so the project list stays data emitted by the partitioner rather than a name hardcoded in YAML.

### Q4 — Coverage output collision: **not live today, documented for when it is**

- `.github/workflows/continuous-integration.yml` sets no `VITEST_COVERAGE` and passes no `--coverage` (grepped; the only `coverage` hits in that file are prose comments and the unrelated weekly test-coverage audit).
- `applications/openthrottle-developer/vitest.config.ts` sets `coverage.provider`/`reportsDirectory` but never `coverage.enabled`, and it does **not** go through the `@tools/dotfiles` factory that implements the `VITEST_COVERAGE=true` gate. Vitest's default is off, so no report is written and the shared `outputs: coverage/applications/openthrottle-developer` is never populated by any shard.
- **If coverage is ever turned on**, three shards writing one `reportsDirectory` will clobber each other and Nx will cache a partial report as if it were whole. The fix at that point is a per-shard `reportsDirectory` plus an explicit merge step — not something to pre-build now.

# Task 4 — driver ids, terminal task statuses, prompt roles

## Driver ids: `Partial` is load-bearing, so the gate moved instead

The task asked whether `Partial<Record<DriverId, AgentDriver>>` is genuinely required or merely
convenient. **It is required, and the file comment is accurate.** `registry/index.ts` must not
import the concrete driver modules — they import `defineDriver` *from* it, so importing them back
closes a cycle. A full `Record<DriverId, AgentDriver>` declared there could therefore never be
satisfied there. `Partial` also keeps `lookupDriver` usable with the trimmed registries the tests
build.

So rather than tighten the type or add the runtime assertion the task offered as a fallback, the
completeness gate moved **one layer up to `drivers/index.ts`, where the imports are already legal**:

```ts
export const DRIVER_REGISTRY = DRIVERS.labelled<AgentDriver>({
  antigravity: antigravityDriver, claude: claudeDriver, /* … */ opencode: opencodeDriver,
});

// derived, so the list and the map cannot drift
export const ALL_DRIVERS: readonly AgentDriver[] = DRIVERS.values.map(
  (id): AgentDriver => DRIVER_REGISTRY[id],
);
```

This is strictly better than the proposed runtime boot assertion: it is a **compile** error, not a
fast failure at boot. `ALL_DRIVERS` was previously a second hand-listed array — adding a driver id
required remembering to touch it — and is now derived, which also closes a gap the task did not
name. `DRIVER_IDS` and `isDriverId` now derive from `DRIVERS`, keeping their exact former types.

## Task statuses: there ARE two representations, and both are legitimate

Flagging this rather than quietly picking one, as instructed. `plan-task-status.constants.ts` is a
well-kept SSOT that declares **two** related unions:

- `PLAN_STATUS` — 8 members, mirrors the Postgres `plan_task_status` enum exactly.
- `TASK_STATUS` — the same set **minus `QUEUED`**, which is plans-only (set when a plan's run is
  enqueued in BullMQ).

This is not an instance of this plan's problem: they are genuinely different sets with a documented
reason, both derived from one file, with a parity test against the migrations. There is also a
separate, unrelated `PLAN_RUN_STATUS` (double-L `CANCELLED`) which the file's own comment warns
against confusing with this one.

`TERMINAL_TASK_STATUSES` lives in a query that updates `Task`, so **`TASK_STATUS` (7 members) is the
correct union** — note the plan body's example sketched 8 including `QUEUED`, which would have been
the wrong one. Added `TASK_STATUS_VOCABULARY` next to the existing constants and converted:

```ts
const TERMINAL_TASK_STATUSES = TASK_STATUS_VOCABULARY.subsetOf({
  [TASK_STATUS.BACKLOG]: false, [TASK_STATUS.BLOCKED]: false,
  [TASK_STATUS.CANCELED]: true, [TASK_STATUS.COMPLETED]: true,
  [TASK_STATUS.IN_PROGRESS]: false, [TASK_STATUS.PENDING]: false,
  [TASK_STATUS.SKIPPED]: true,
});
```

The call site spreads it (`[...TERMINAL_TASK_STATUSES]`) into the query builder, which works
unchanged on a `ReadonlySet` — the task-1 return-shape decision holds up at a real call site.

The pacing risk the task named turned out to be the least of it. First take was **224 seconds**. Breaking that down surfaced four defects, three of which silently affect every video already recorded:

1. **150s of it was a hung region sample.** `sampleRegion` used Playwright's 30s default `boundingBox` timeout, and a miss leaves the beat unsampled so it retries on EVERY step of that beat. My `restart` ROI pointed at `#shell-banner`, which is not on the surface the beat opens on. Five steps, five 30-second waits, nothing in the log. Now 1.5s.
2. **41s was typing the add-json command.** A 500-character JSON command line typed at 50wpm is both untrue to how anyone runs it (you were just told to COPY it) and most of the short's budget. It arrives pasted now — same string, from the same source as the highlighted line.
3. **Narration was playing against the wrong picture.** `planTimeline` matches narration to flow beats POSITIONALLY, so a flow beat with no narration row does not go unnarrated — it eats the slot and every later beat inherits the previous line. I had eight beats for the script's seven rows, and a take shipped where "and there it is, in the dashboard" played five seconds before the dashboard. Merged the beat, and `planTimeline` now warns on a count mismatch rather than misaligning quietly.
4. **The payoff was being cut off.** `-shortest` on the body mux truncated the picture to the narration track, which ends at its last cue — so any flow holding on its payoff after the last line lost that hold. Fifteen seconds, ending on the plans table. `-af apad` fixes it.

Then two frame-accounting bugs that made played time disagree with recorded time by 6 seconds — which is the assumption every narration cue rests on. The concat demuxer ignores the FINAL entry's duration and hands that entry the PREVIOUS one's, so the repeated tail frame duplicated the whole closing hold (measured on a synthetic list: 2s + 3s assembled to 8.00s, 5.07s after the fix). And the closing dwell was held for a nominal 40ms rather than until the flow ended. Net: a 53.3s capture now yields a 53.3s picture, against 59.5s before.

## Task 3 — build-completeness guard (fail fast + consume-time gate)

**Guard script:** `scripts/verify-dist-complete.ts` (reusable, takes `<projectRoot>`). Walks `src/` for emitting modules (excludes `.d.ts`, `*.spec.*`, `*.test.*`, `__tests__`/`__mocks__`), and asserts each has a non-empty compiled `.js` under the package's `outDir` (read from tsconfig.lib.json; checks both `dist/src/...` and `dist/...` so it's layout-agnostic for the sibling audit). Exits 1 listing the missing modules, with a message pointing at the purge runbook.

**Two wiring points (defense in depth):**
1. **Build-time (self-heal, task 2):** the build command runs the guard and force-rebuilds on failure → a truncated dist is never cached on a cache-WRITE.
2. **Consume-time (fail-fast, this task):** a per-package `verify-dist-complete` Nx target, `cache: false`, `dependsOn: [build]`, mirroring `verify-graphql-codegen`. Because it's `cache:false`, it ALWAYS runs even when `build` gets a cache-HIT — so if a previously-poisoned entry is restored from GCS, the guard runs against the truncated dist and FAILS with a clear message instead of the cryptic downstream "Cannot find module …/workflow.js". Wired into root `check:local:verify` via `nx run-many --target=verify-dist-complete --all`.

**Validation:** guard exits 0 on the complete 52-module dist; exits 1 naming `src/utils/workflow.ts` when that `.js` is removed. New/edited files pass `prettier --check`.

## Task 6 — BLOCKED: Monaco is not in this chunk, and ≤80 KB is not reachable

### The `EditorWindow`/Monaco premise is false
Fingerprinting the built `plans._planId._index-*.js` (232.8 KB):

| token | occurrences |
|---|---:|
| `monaco` | **0** |
| `acorn` / `micromark` | 0 |

Monaco is **never bundled** — `@monaco-editor/react` loads it from `cdn.jsdelivr.net` at runtime (see task 3). And `EditorWindow` is already its own **14.5 KB** chunk (`EditorWindow-2cpYbudo.js`), not inlined into the route. Lazy-loading it could move at most 14.5 KB, nowhere near the 147 KB the acceptance needs.

### What the 232.8 KB actually is
Splitting the chunk by its longest emitted lines:

| Content | KB |
|---|---:|
| Plan-detail feature code (tabs, tables, run config, hooks, transparency panel) | ~134 |
| **Zod** (`z` core + v4 JSON-Schema converter — `metadataRegistry`, `reused === 'ref'`, `cycles`) | **~72** |
| misc | ~27 |

The zod comes from `app/routing/plans/utils/workflow-ralph-validate.ts` → `RalphPlanRunTuningInputSchema` from `~/__generated__/schemas`. That is **genuine client-side work**: it validates the workflow-ralph run-options UI state live as the user edits, mirroring `tools/workflows/src/utils/parsers.ts`. Removing it means rewriting validation, not code-splitting.

I confirmed the server-only path is already clean: the eleven action helpers imported from `~/routing/plans/actions/planId` (which imports `zod/v3`) are referenced **only** inside the route's `action` export, and React Router correctly strips them from the client build — that zod copy is not what is in the chunk.

The app packages already declare `sideEffects: false` (all four), so this is not a tree-shaking gap.

### Larger real cost on this route
The route's full static graph is **1292.8 KB**, and **505.6 KB of it is `MarkdownRenderer`** — 39%. That is the genuine win available here, and it is already filed as **task 11**. On this route markdown rendering is legitimate (plan descriptions), so the fix there is scoping it out of the *shell*, not off this route.

### Needs a decision
1. **Re-baseline** to ~160 KB (achievable only if client-side run-option validation moves server-side) or accept ~233 KB as the floor for this feature page.
2. **Lazy-load `EditorWindow`** anyway — worth 14.5 KB on the Output/Tasks tabs, adds a Suspense boundary. I did not do it unprompted since it neither meets the acceptance nor pays for its complexity.
3. Treat **task 11** as the real fix for this route's first-load cost.

## Task 3 — Partitioner taught about per-suite sharding

### Shape chosen: **B — shard-aware partition.** A rejected.

**Why B.** The partitioner already owns the answer to "who runs what", and it is the only place that has the affected list in hand. Shape A would have moved two pieces of that knowledge into YAML — the sharded project's *name*, and whether it is *affected this run* — and the second one is not free: the workflow cannot know it without its own `nx show projects --affected` call, i.e. a second graph computation per box on a repo that is actively optimising CI cost. A also has to teach the round-trip check an *exception*, which is precisely the wrong direction for a guard whose entire job is to be unforgiving.

**What B costs:** a second output channel. Paid for by switching stdout from one bare line to `key=value` lines, which is strictly more legible than the alternative of positional fields and keeps the property the old header cared about — **no emitted value can contain a space**, so nothing word-splits on the way into a shell variable. There is a unit test asserting exactly that.

### stdout contract (all four keys always emitted; empty value = nothing to do)

```
selector=!openthrottle-developer,!@openthrottle/react-router-chat   # lint/typecheck: unchanged partition
testSelector=!@openthrottle/react-router-chat                       # test: same chunk, sharded app removed
suiteShard=2/3                                                      # this box's Vitest --shard
suiteShardProjects=openthrottle-developer                           # what to run under it
```

### The two axes, kept separate

`SUITE_SHARDED_PROJECTS` (currently just `openthrottle-developer`) is a roster, not a special case buried in a conditional. A project on it is **still dealt to exactly one chunk** — `distributeEvenly` is untouched, so its lint and typecheck still belong to one box, as the task required. It is lifted out only of `testSelector`, downstream of the deal, and picked up instead by a `--shard` invocation that runs on **every** box.

Pulling it out of the deal entirely would have been the tempting simplification and is wrong: it would drop its lint/typecheck off every box, which is the exact silent-green failure this script exists to prevent.

### Round-trip guarantee: strengthened, not excepted

`verifyShardSelection()` now round-trips **both** selectors through Nx, via a shared `verifySelection(label, grouping)` that names which one failed. The carve-out is checked as its *own* grouping rather than being allowed to surface as a mismatch against the partition. Widening `unexpected` to tolerate the sharded project would have blunted the guard for every *other* project too; checking the carved-out set separately keeps it exact on both. `getShardSelectionErrors()` itself is unchanged — it is still the pure comparator, now called twice. A regression test asserts a genuine drop from the carved-out grouping still errors, and still does not mention the sharded app.

### Verified end-to-end against real Nx (developer app artificially made affected, 3 boxes)

```
box 1: selector=!monorepo               testSelector=!monorepo   suiteShard=1/3
box 2: selector=!openthrottle-developer  testSelector=(empty)     suiteShard=2/3
box 3: selector=(empty)                  testSelector=(empty)     suiteShard=3/3
```

Box 2 drew the developer app, so it lints and typechecks it and its `testSelector` is empty. Box 3 drew nothing at all and still owes a third of the developer files — the **new third state** task 4 has to make legible in the log. With the developer app *not* affected, all three boxes emit `suiteShard=` / `suiteShardProjects=` empty and nothing shards.

### Noted, not acted on

`distributeEvenly`'s applications-first bias is now balancing a deal whose heaviest member contributes only its lint/typecheck weight to `test`. Recorded in the function's JSDoc; **not** re-tuned here, because re-tuning it wants per-project timing data this script still does not have.

### Validation

`pnpm nx run monorepo:test` → **15 files / 231 tests passed**. `monorepo:lint` and `monorepo:typecheck` green. New cases cover: the sharded app affected vs not; `selector` vs `testSelector` divergence on the box that drew it and equality on the boxes that did not; every box getting its own `suiteShard`; an empty chunk that still shards; coverage-exactly-once for lint/typecheck **and** for test counting the shard; the `key=value` rendering including the no-spaces property.

**Decision: reconcile at boot**, not "wait for the next apply".

The task offered the natural-heal option as the simplest, and it was rejected on evidence. Surveying `repository_checkouts` showed the residue is **7 real repos**, not the one in the original report:

```
atlasworks, atlasworks/services/native-apps, .../nativeapps,

```

Natural healing requires the user to re-apply editor config in each — something they have no reason to do and no way to know they should. That is "silently dirty with no path forward" wearing a different hat.

### Implementation

`WorkspaceEditorConfigService.reconcileManifestExclusions()` walks every registered checkout, and writes the exclude for those that already carry a manifest. Wired into the same boot lifecycle as the foreign-skill reconcile, with **its own try/catch** — different feature, different block, and one failing must not take the other down (covered by a test).

It never touches the manifest itself. That is the identity anchor `RepositoryInspectionService` reads to reconcile a moved folder, so healing must leave it exactly where it is — asserted explicitly rather than assumed.

## Task 2 — ROOT CAUSE: `requestAnimationFrame` starvation in a hidden tab. **Not a product bug.**

### The chain of evidence

**Step 1 — narrowed to animation, not colour/radius/sizing.** A scratch story rendered raw recharts (no `ChartContainer`, fixed `width`/`height`, literal `fill="#8884d8"`):

| probe | config | shapes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a | Bar, literal fill, animation default | **0** |
| b | Bar, literal fill, `isAnimationActive={false}` | **3** |
| c | Bar, `radius={[4,4,0,0]}`, `isAnimationActive={false}` | **3** |
| d | Pie, animation default | **0** |
| e | Pie, `isAnimationActive={false}` | **3** |

So `fill`, the `radius` tuple, `Cell`, and `ChartContainer` are all innocent — it is purely the entry animation. Re-checked long after mount: still 0, so it is stalled, not mid-flight.

**Step 2 — found the mechanism in recharts source.** `animation/JavascriptAnimate.js` does `useState(isActive ? 0 : 1)` and only advances via `animationControllerImpl`, which drives ticks through `RequestAnimationFrameTimeoutController` — a `requestAnimationFrame` loop. If rAF never fires, the interpolation value stays at **0** forever. At t=0 recharts `Rectangle`/`Sector` have zero size/angle and return `null` — exactly the empty `.recharts-inactive-bar` / empty `.recharts-pie` layers observed.

**Step 3 — measured rAF directly.** In the Browser-pane tab:

```
framesIn500ms: 0
document.visibilityState: "hidden"
```

**rAF fires zero times because the automation tab is never visible.** Browsers do not run rAF in hidden tabs.

**Step 4 — proved causality.** Replacing `requestAnimationFrame` with a `setTimeout` shim before mount, changing nothing else, flipped every probe from 0 to 3. Then applying the same shim in `.storybook/preview.tsx` and loading the **real, unmodified** stories:

- `SimpleBarChart → Default` — bars render, rounded top corners from the `radius` tuple, correct `var(--color-*)` colour
- `SimplePieChart → Default` — all sectors render in theme colours
- `SimpleLineChart → Default` — line renders

### The plan's premise is wrong in two ways

1. **There is no defect in `SimpleBarChart` or `SimplePieChart`.** All three candidate causes are disproved: not a version regression (3.10.1 behaves correctly once rAF runs), not component misuse (raw recharts with literal fills fails identically), not React 19 (recharts 3.10.1 declares `^19.0.0` support and works fine).

2. **"Line and Area are unaffected" is incorrect.** They are equally starved; counting paths just hides it. `SimpleLineChart`'s curve had `stroke-dasharray="0px 487.46px"` — the path exists but draws **zero** length, so the screenshot showed dots and no line. `SimpleAreaChart` rendered **completely blank**. The original "1 curve path / 2 area paths" evidence counted DOM nodes rather than looking at pixels.

### Consequence for the fix

The correct action is **not** to change the components. Disabling animation or pinning recharts would degrade working code to satisfy a measurement artifact. What is actually owed:

- remove the `⚠️ KNOWN ISSUE` blocks, which document a non-existent bug
- document the rAF/hidden-tab trap in the workbench so this is not re-filed by the next agent that inspects Storybook through automation

Tasks 3 and 4 are being rewritten accordingly.

## Task — Stop equating exit code 0 with task success

### Design decision: **new terminal status `no_op`**, fed by an opt-in agent-emitted sentinel

The task asked to weigh a distinct terminal status against a nullable outcome column, and to prefer a structured CLI signal over prose sniffing. Investigating the options changed the answer to the second part.

**A structured CLI signal cannot solve this.** The plan suggested `--output-format stream-json` gives a typed result event we could read. It does — but a result event reports that *the turn completed*, and a turn in which the model explicitly declines the task **is** a completed turn as far as the CLI is concerned. Run `479b58d1` would have emitted a perfectly healthy `success` result event. The CLI genuinely does not know whether the work happened; only the agent does. So no amount of output-format plumbing yields the signal, and root cause 3's format change stays fully out of scope.

**Why a status value rather than a side column.** The plan's user-visible requirement is that an aborted run be *distinguishable at a glance in the history list*, and the history table renders `status`. A parallel column means every existing consumer that switches on `status` keeps asserting "succeeded" — the lie stays in the data model and each reader has to remember to check a second field. Adding the value fixes it once, at the source. It was also cheaper than the plan assumed: `status` is a `TEXT` column with a `CHECK` constraint and GraphQL exposes it as `String`, not an enum, so there is no enum type to regenerate — only the constraint and a description.

**Why opt-in.** `no_op` is populated only when the agent emits an explicit sentinel. A job that says nothing keeps precisely its old mapping, so no existing job's behavior and no historical row changes meaning. This is the "explicit convention the job prompt opts into" the task endorsed — a declared machine token, not regex-sniffing model prose.

### The protocol

```
OT_RUN_OUTCOME: completed   → succeeded
OT_RUN_OUTCOME: no_op       → no_op
(absent)                    → unchanged (exit-code mapping)
```

Hardening, each with a test:
- **Line-anchored and case-sensitive** (`/^OT_RUN_OUTCOME:[ \t]*(completed|no_op)[ \t]*$/gmu`), so the token appearing mid-sentence in prose cannot trip it.
- **Last occurrence wins**, so a prompt that quotes the protocol while explaining it cannot outvote the agent's real verdict at the end.
- **Only ever overrides `ok`.** A timeout, cancel, or non-zero exit is already reported honestly, and a sentinel printed just before a crash must not upgrade a `failed` run.
- **Unknown verdict values are ignored** (treated as no claim) rather than guessed at.

`no_op` is terminal and **is not an error** — `failed` stays reserved for non-zero exit, timeout, and spawn failure. That distinction is written into the migration comment, the entity JSDoc, and the GraphQL description so it survives.

**The audit's diagnosis was wrong.** `settings-*.js` (1229.7 KB) was NOT `GlobalAnimationMesh`/`GlobalAnimationWaves` — those are ~4 KB canvas wrappers. Fingerprinting the built chunk showed **171 radix references + 9 recharts references** and zero `@paper-design/shaders` code.

**Verdict: path B (Playwright), and specifically a CDP screencast resampled to a constant 30fps — NOT Playwright `recordVideo`.** The plan's going-in recommendation was B; the spike confirms it, but with a material correction inside B that the plan did not anticipate.

Both paths drove the same reference demo (sign in -> create a plan -> see it in the list) against a PRODUCTION build of openthrottle-developer on :7180 with the real server on :7181. Spike code + verdict committed at `applications/openthrottle-developer/tests/demo/spike/` (`README.md` has the full write-up); artifacts land in `spike/output/` and are gitignored.

**Path A rejected — both halves failed, not just the known gaps.**
- Capture: `ffmpeg -f avfoundation -i "4"` for a 2-second test HUNG INDEFINITELY and produced no file. macOS gates screen capture behind an interactive per-binary Screen Recording grant. A recorder that needs someone to click a system dialog is not a pipeline. It is also macOS-only, cannot run headless, and records the ENTIRE DESKTOP — a leak vector aimed straight at the control task 9 exists to build.
- Driver: the Maestro flow failed on its first assertion with a hard crash in Maestro's own web driver — `CdpWebDriver.deviceInfo NullPointerException: null cannot be cast to non-null type kotlin.Int`. Maestro Web (Beta, CLI 2.0.9) cannot read the view hierarchy in this environment at all.

**Path B measured, twice, headless, no flakes:**

| | recordVideo | CDP screencast -> ffmpeg |
| --- | --- | --- |
| codec | VP8/WebM | H.264/MP4 |
| frame rate | 25fps, NOT configurable | constant 30fps |
| size (~32s) | 2.4 MB | 732 KB (262 MB intermediate frames) |
| text at 1:1 | crisp | crisp |
| hold a frame for narration | no | yes |

Text crispness is a wash — cropped 1:1 regions from both are clean, and the VP8 intermediate did not visibly hurt type. The decision turns entirely on frame-rate control and pacing, where recordVideo has no knobs.

**The frame-timestamp detail is the whole trick.** CDP emits a frame only when the page changes, so a naive `-framerate N` assembly plays idle stretches fast and busy stretches slow. The recorder stores `frame.metadata.timestamp` per frame and emits an ffmpeg `concat` list with real per-frame durations; `fps=30` resamples to constant. A deliberate dwell becomes one long-duration frame — exactly the pacing control the spec demands and path A cannot provide.

**Severity is the design, and it is the part worth arguing with.** The task asked for the documented conventions to be enforced. Enforced strictly, they fail **every episode in the season**: 22 of 24 miss a baseline tag, all 24 sit outside the 6–10 tag range, and neither long-form has chapters. So a rule is one of two things:

- **error** — structurally wrong for any episode, draft or not: over budget, non-monotonic beats, cues running backwards, a duplicate release slot, a `selectedVariant` naming nothing, a short carrying chapters or a designed thumbnail.
- **publish** — a documented convention that is advisory on a `draft` and an error once the episode is `ready` or `published`.

That makes the tag baseline bind exactly when it matters. Nobody can mark an episode ready until it carries the five tags, and the drift stays visible in the meantime rather than being dropped. **Today: 24 episodes, 0 errors, 47 advisory.**

If you would rather the conventions block immediately, it is a one-line change of severity per rule — but then the first `check:local` run fails on all 24 and someone has to write 22 tag lists before anything else lands.

Task 11 (publishing cadence and metadata workflow) — done. `docs/marketing/publishing.md`.

**Cadence: two a week, sustained.** Not an arbitrary number — it is what the pipeline can actually keep up with. Machine time is 8-9 minutes per video once its flow exists, but a NEW FLOW costs tens of minutes of human authoring. The flow is the bottleneck, not the rendering, and that is what caps the rate.

**Release order** is in each script's front matter (the authority) and tabulated in the doc with a reason per position. Head: 1 -> 3 -> 2 -> L2 -> 11 -> 5 -> 21. The flagship long-form is **22nd of 24**, deliberately: it is ten minutes, depends on a replayed run, and is the video where a rough voice or a stale UI hurts most, so it should ship after the format is proven twenty times. Tail: worktrees (23) and kill-a-run (24), both still constrained by what the app shows.

**Playlists:** four, mirroring the script groups. Long-form goes in the playlist matching its subject, not a separate "long videos" bin — viewers sort by topic, not duration.

**Metadata is never retyped.** `metadata.json` comes out of the assembly stage from the script's own front matter, so the YouTube title cannot drift from the title the video was built to demonstrate. Upload the `.srt` every time — Shorts autoplay silently and burned-in captions do not help search.

**Cross-posting:** the 9:16 master carries no YouTube-specific branding by design, so it goes anywhere unchanged. Stronger recommendation in the doc: **embed each Short in the `docs/` page it explains, as it publishes**, not as a later sweep. A video that earns its keep as documentation is worth twice as much.

**Upload automation: the trigger condition is already partly met, and the recommendation still stands.** The task said keep uploads manual until the checklist catches at least one real problem. It has: the pilot's script claimed a linked-commit view with the task id in its footer, a surface that does not exist in the app. First video, exactly the failure mode the checklist exists for — and caught by a human reading the script against the app, not by any automated check. An automated uploader would have published it.

So the bar is met once. ## Task 1 — Locked helper API for @openthrottle/react-router-utils

Surveyed every call site. Success envelope in the wild is `{ ok: true }` (no `error` field) and failure is `{ ok: false, error: string }` (skills.$slug / write-skill-file.server), while settings/notes/schedule actions return a looser `{ error?: string }` (no `ok`). So a *loose error reader* is behaviorally identical to the `ok === false` gate everywhere it's used.

### Types — `src/utils/action-result.ts`
- `interface ActionFailure { ok: false; error: string }`
- `type ActionSuccess<T = unknown> = { ok: true } & T`
- `type ActionResult<T = unknown> = ActionSuccess<T> | ActionFailure`

### Functions — `src/utils/action-result.ts` (pure)
- `getActionError(data: unknown): string | undefined` — the shared `data != null && typeof data === 'object' && 'error' in data && typeof data.error === 'string' && length>0` reader. Envelope-agnostic; covers both `{ ok, error }` and `{ error }`. Returns `undefined` for empty strings / non-objects / null. Call sites wanting `null` do `getActionError(x) ?? null`.
- `isActionFailure(data: unknown): data is ActionFailure` — narrows `ok === false` with a non-empty string `error`.
- `isActionSuccess(data: unknown): boolean` — `ok === true` (rounds out the `'ok' in` sites: SettingsKeysRevokeCell, PlanTasksBoard).

### Fetcher helpers — `src/utils/fetcher.ts` (pure)
Typed via `import type { Fetcher } from 'react-router'` (union of state variants, each carrying `state` + `formData`).
- `isFetcherBusy(fetcher: Fetcher): boolean` — `fetcher.state !== 'idle'`.
- `isFetcherFormPending(fetcher: Fetcher, field: string): boolean` — busy AND `fetcher.formData?.get(field)` is a non-empty string (skills.$slug `intent`).

No `useFetcherAction` hook — a wrapper would hide `useFetcher` for no gain; helpers stay pure/typed. GraphQL `{ data, errors }` parsing stays in `react-router-graphql`; **no GraphQL imports here**. `react` + `react-router` become peerDependencies (task 2).

## Task 4 — SSR `ide-engine.server` 11674.2 KB → 25.7 KB ✅

### Cause
The chunk was the **TypeScript compiler**, pulled in via `ts-morph` (fingerprints in the built chunk: `TypeChecker` ×204, `ScriptTarget` ×165, `createProgram` ×71). `ts-morph` is a dependency of `@openthrottle/openthrottle-ide`, and Vite was bundling it into the SSR output.

### Fix
`ssr.external: ['ts-morph']` in `applications/openthrottle-developer/vite.config.ts`. Node resolves it from `node_modules` on the first request that needs symbol analysis; routes already reach the adapter through a dynamic `import()`, so nothing about the load pattern changed.

`@openthrottle/openthrottle-ide` itself stays **bundled** on purpose — it is source-first (`main: ./src/index.ts`), so an externalized Node `import` would hit raw TypeScript at runtime.

### Required companion change
Externalizing alone would have **broken the IDE routes**. The emitted chunk does `from "ts-morph"`, but the developer app never declared it — it was a transitive dep of `openthrottle-ide`, and pnpm's strict layout makes it unresolvable from the app directory:

```
ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND  Cannot find package 'ts-morph' imported from .../build/server/
```

So `"ts-morph": "catalog:"` was added to the app's dependencies. Re-verified after `pnpm install`: `import('ts-morph')` from `build/server/` resolves with **540 exports**.

### Measured (production build, `--skip-nx-cache`)
| | Audit baseline | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| `ide-engine.server-*.js` | 11674.2 KB / 2042.7 gz | **25.7 KB / 6.8 gz** |
| Server build dir | 25 MB | **4.9 MB** |
| Server JS total | — | **0.31 MB** |

Acceptance: chunk ≤ 2048 KB → **25.7 KB** ✅; server dir ≤ 15 MB → **4.9 MB** ✅
(The server-dir figure also benefits from task 3 removing the copied Monaco workers.)
